Urban/peri-urban residents with improved infrastructure access. These individuals have water piped into their homes or compounds, reflecting better access to municipal water systems or private boreholes common in towns and cities.

Rural residents with compound-level water access. These people rely on water sources located within their compound boundaries, such as hand-dug wells or rainwater collection systems, which is typical for rural areas with some development.

Remote or underserved rural residents dependent on external water sources. These individuals must travel outside their compounds to access water from communal boreholes, rivers, or other distant sources, reflecting limited infrastructure in their areas.
Uncertain or non-responsive respondents. These people either don't know where their main water source is located or refuse to answer, possibly due to confusion about the question or privacy concerns.
Residents with no reliable water access. A small segment lacks consistent access to any formal water source and may rely on unsafe or irregular supplies.

Family-centered traditionalists (35%): Women who place extremely high value on family bonds and kinship networks, viewing relatives as the most trustworthy people in their lives due to cultural emphasis on extended family loyalty.

Moderately trusting pragmatists (40%): Women who trust their relatives quite a bit but maintain some realistic caution, recognizing that family relationships vary in quality and that not all relatives are equally dependable.
Cautious skeptics (15%): Women who have experienced family conflict or betrayal and therefore trust relatives only somewhat, distinguishing between close immediate family and more distant relatives.
Guarded minimalists (8%): Women who have limited family support systems or difficult family histories, trusting relatives only a little or not at all.
Uncertain respondents (2%): Women who are unsure how to characterize their trust in relatives or decline to answer, possibly due to complex family situations.
Urban/semi-urban residents with stable employment or business interests who have invested in home infrastructure and have reliable electricity access from the national grid.
Rural residents in areas with limited grid infrastructure who lack electric connections and rely on alternative energy sources like generators, solar panels, or kerosene lamps.
Residents in transitional areas with inconsistent or unreliable grid connections who may have formal connections but experience frequent outages and service interruptions.
Lower-income urban dwellers living in informal settlements or rental properties who cannot afford to establish or maintain formal electrical connections despite proximity to grid infrastructure.

Individuals uncertain about their electricity situation or unwilling to provide clear answers, possibly due to concerns about taxation, informal arrangements, or lack of clear knowledge about their connection status.
Urban, internet-connected women who follow news regularly and are informed about international affairs. They are likely aware of Japan's development assistance programs to Senegal.
Women with moderate news consumption through television but limited internet access who have some general awareness of foreign aid but lack specific knowledge about Japan's role.
Women with minimal news consumption and very limited internet access who have not heard about Japan's development assistance to Senegal.
Women who are engaged with current events through television but skeptical of government narratives, who may be uncertain whether Japan's assistance actually reaches ordinary citizens.
Women who prefer not to answer or genuinely have no opinion on international relations and foreign aid matters.

Skeptical critics who believe the government is mishandling key issues like corruption and feel the country is heading in the wrong direction. They tend to be politically disengaged and pessimistic about national progress.
Cautious optimists who acknowledge government problems but see some positive developments and believe the country could be moving in the right direction with continued effort.
Uncertain and uninformed citizens who lack sufficient knowledge about national affairs and government performance, making them hesitant to judge the country's overall direction.

Moderate pragmatists who recognize mixed results in government performance—some areas handled fairly well, others poorly—and hold a balanced view that the country's direction is neither clearly right nor wrong.
Disengaged non-responders who are unwilling or unable to express a clear opinion about the country's direction, reflecting broader political apathy or disconnection from national discourse.
Urban residents with regular internet access who are more informed about health matters and have had direct exposure to COVID-19 cases in their communities or families.
Rural or semi-rural residents with limited healthcare access who may not have been tested or diagnosed despite potential exposure, and are less likely to have confirmed cases in their awareness.
Economically vulnerable individuals experiencing cash income instability who lack resources for testing or medical care, making it difficult to confirm COVID-19 cases even if illness occurred.
Younger, more digitally connected individuals who are more likely to have sought testing and have clearer knowledge of whether they or household members contracted COVID-19.
Older or more traditional community members who may be hesitant to discuss health matters or uncertain about distinguishing COVID-19 from other illnesses without formal diagnosis.

Urban professionals with higher internet usage and exposure to diverse perspectives. They tend to be tolerant of different groups and would likely not care or somewhat like having homosexual neighbours, viewing sexual orientation as a personal matter.

Religiously conservative individuals who hold traditional values and view homosexuality as contrary to their faith beliefs. They would likely somewhat dislike or strongly dislike having homosexual neighbours.

Pragmatic moderates who are not strongly ideological and focus on practical community concerns. They would likely not care about neighbours' sexual orientation as long as it doesn't affect community harmony.
Younger, more cosmopolitan individuals influenced by global media and internet exposure who actively support LGBTQ+ acceptance. They would strongly like or somewhat like having homosexual neighbours.

Rural or less-connected individuals with limited exposure to LGBTQ+ issues who hold traditional community norms. They would likely somewhat dislike homosexual neighbours based on unfamiliarity and cultural conservatism.

Urban middle-class households with stable employment and resources. They have modern in-house toilets as a standard feature of their homes, viewing adequate sanitation as a basic necessity they have already secured.

Working-class urban residents with modest incomes who have invested in compound toilets. They have access to sanitation facilities within their property boundaries, though not always inside the main house, representing a practical middle ground.

Lower-income urban dwellers in informal settlements or rental accommodations with limited resources. They rely on outside toilets or shared facilities outside their compounds, facing constraints due to housing insecurity or affordability.

Residents in newly developed urban areas or those in transition between housing situations. They may lack any toilet facility currently available, though they aspire to improve their sanitation access as their circumstances improve.

A small segment unwilling or unable to provide clear information about their sanitation situation. They either refuse to answer or genuinely lack knowledge about available facilities in their living space.

Skeptical urbanites disillusioned with government performance. They see corruption as rampant and poorly addressed, making them believe the country is heading in the wrong direction despite some economic activity in cities.
Cautiously optimistic citizens who acknowledge problems but see some government efforts and potential for improvement, viewing the country's direction as generally right despite current challenges.
Politically engaged party supporters who align with the current government's vision and policies, believing the country is moving in the right direction regardless of specific criticisms.

Uncertain or disengaged urban residents who lack sufficient information about national direction and government performance, unable to form a clear opinion on whether things are improving or declining.

Pragmatic citizens focused on immediate urban concerns (employment, services, security) who see mixed signals—some improvements in city infrastructure but persistent corruption and inequality—leaving them ambivalent about overall direction.
Daily TV news watchers who rely on television as their primary news source, reflecting traditional media consumption habits common in Zimbabwe.
Regular but not daily TV viewers who watch a few times a week, balancing television with other news sources in their routine.
Occasional TV news consumers who watch a few times a month or less, preferring other sources or having limited access to reliable electricity.
Non-television news users who never watch TV for news, either due to lack of access, preference for internet/radio, or economic constraints.
Those who refuse to answer or don't know their viewing habits, a small segment with unclear media consumption patterns.

Urban middle-class professionals and business owners with stable incomes who live in well-developed neighborhoods with reliable electricity infrastructure. They have electric connections and view reliable power as essential for their work and quality of life.

Lower-income urban residents in established neighborhoods with basic infrastructure who have electric connections, though they may experience occasional outages or unreliable service. They depend on electricity but struggle with affordability and consistency.

Informal sector workers and recent migrants to urban areas living in peripheral neighborhoods or informal settlements without formal electric connections. They lack access to grid electricity and rely on alternative sources like generators or kerosene.

Residents in transitional urban areas where electricity infrastructure is incomplete or unreliable, with some having connections while others do not. They experience inconsistent access and view electrification as an ongoing development priority.

Households that are uncertain about their electricity status or unwilling to answer, possibly due to concerns about taxation or informal connections. They represent a small segment with ambiguous or undeclared electricity access.
Rural subsistence farmers with no internet access or electricity. They have never used the internet and get news exclusively through radio, word-of-mouth, or occasional television when available.
Urban poor and semi-urban residents with very limited internet access. They rarely use the internet, accessing it less than once a month at internet cafes or through borrowed phones.
Young urban residents and traders with moderate smartphone access. They use the internet a few times a week, primarily through mobile data, to check news and social media.
Relatively affluent urban dwellers with regular internet connectivity. They use the internet daily or nearly daily for news, business, and communication.
Occasional internet users in transitional circumstances. They access the internet a few times a month when they have money for data or visit locations with WiFi.

Rural agricultural workers and subsistence farmers with irregular income from seasonal work, who experience frequent periods without cash income due to the unpredictable nature of farming and herding in Mauritania's harsh climate.
Urban informal sector workers and day laborers in cities like Nouakchott who have sporadic employment and regularly go without cash income between irregular job opportunities.
Salaried government employees and formal sector workers with stable monthly income who rarely or never experience periods without cash, though they may face occasional delays in payment.
Small business owners and traders with modest but relatively consistent income from commerce who occasionally face cash flow problems but generally maintain income throughout the year.
Unemployed or underemployed individuals, particularly youth, who frequently or constantly lack cash income and depend on family support or irregular assistance.

Urban/peri-urban residents with improved infrastructure access. These individuals have water sources inside or within their compound, reflecting better access to piped water or protected wells from investments in urban water systems.

Rural residents with moderate water access. These people rely on water sources within their compound, typically from hand-dug wells or rainwater collection systems, representing the majority rural experience in Ethiopia.

Remote/underserved rural populations with limited water infrastructure. These individuals must travel outside their compound to access water from communal sources like rivers, springs, or distant boreholes due to lack of local infrastructure.

Affluent urban households with premium water access. These people have piped water directly inside their homes, representing the small elite segment with access to municipal water systems or private connections.
Pessimistic citizens who believe the country faces serious challenges and is moving in the wrong direction, particularly concerned about corruption and governance issues.
Cautiously optimistic individuals who see some positive developments and believe the country is generally heading in the right direction despite existing problems.
Uncertain citizens who lack sufficient information or have mixed views about the country's direction and prefer not to commit to a clear position.
Pragmatic observers who acknowledge both significant problems and some progress, viewing the country's direction as complex and difficult to characterize simply.
Disengaged individuals who rarely discuss or follow national matters closely and have limited opinions on the country's overall direction.
Family-centered traditionalists (35%): Strong Catholic values with deep emphasis on kinship bonds; trust relatives completely as the foundation of social life and moral support.
Moderately trusting community members (30%): Believe in family loyalty but recognize some variation in trustworthiness among relatives; generally trust relatives a lot with occasional reservations.
Cautious pragmatists (20%): Have experienced family conflicts or economic pressures that create some skepticism; trust relatives somewhat but maintain healthy boundaries.
Skeptical individuals (10%): Due to personal experiences with family disputes or betrayals, trust relatives only a little or with significant reservations.
Uncertain respondents (5%): Lack clear perspective on the question or prefer not to answer definitively about family trust dynamics.
Rural subsistence farmers with minimal cash income integration who regularly face periods without any cash earnings, viewing this as a normal part of their seasonal agricultural cycle.
Urban informal sector workers and day laborers who experience frequent income gaps between irregular jobs, struggling with unpredictable cash flow several times throughout the year.
Households with at least one stable formal or semi-formal employment source who rarely go without cash income, though they may occasionally face brief gaps during transitions.
Families dependent on remittances or irregular income sources who experience periodic cash shortages but not constantly, managing through extended family networks and informal savings.
Extremely vulnerable households in chronic poverty who are always or nearly always without reliable cash income, surviving through barter, aid, and community support.
Politically disengaged workers who never discuss politics with family or friends and feel no connection to any political party, viewing politics as irrelevant to their daily lives.
Employed individuals with limited political awareness who lack sufficient information about parties and their platforms, resulting in genuine uncertainty about whether they feel close to any party.
Pragmatic full-time workers who feel some connection to a political party, typically based on perceived benefits to their employment or economic interests rather than ideological commitment.
Civically aware employees who actively avoid party affiliation despite exposure to political information, preferring independence and skepticism toward political institutions.
Individuals unwilling to disclose their political party preferences due to social sensitivity or fear of judgment in their workplace or community.
Urban employed women with stable incomes, living in cities like Gaborone or Francistown, who own or have access to motor vehicles for work and personal transportation.
Rural and semi-rural women with limited incomes who do not own motor vehicles but may have family members who own motorcycles or vehicles for farming or business purposes.
Working-class women in towns and villages who rely on public transportation and do not personally own vehicles, though some household members may own motorcycles.
Wealthier women in urban areas who personally own motor vehicles as a status symbol and necessity for their professional and social lives.
Young women in rural areas with minimal economic resources who have no access to personal or household motor vehicles and rely entirely on walking or public transport.
Rural subsistence farmers with limited resources who cannot afford a television and have no household members who own one, reflecting the economic constraints common in many Ghanaian communities.
Lower-income households where a family member owns a television but the respondent personally does not, representing shared household assets in extended family arrangements typical in Ghana.
Relatively better-off individuals who personally own a television, often urban or semi-urban residents with stable income who can afford personal electronics.

Older adults in mixed-income households who rely on television as a primary news source (as shown in the news consumption data) and benefit from household television ownership even if they don't personally own it.
A small segment of respondents who are uncertain about household television ownership or decline to answer, reflecting either cognitive limitations or privacy concerns.
Politically disengaged citizens who rarely discuss politics and feel no connection to any party, viewing political affiliation as irrelevant to their daily lives.
Pragmatic non-partisans who are aware of political matters but consciously choose not to align with any particular party, preferring independence in their political views.
Party-affiliated individuals who feel close to a particular political party, likely due to shared values, community ties, or perceived benefits from that party's policies.
Uncertain citizens who are unsure whether they feel close to any party, possibly due to limited political knowledge or ambivalence about available political options.
Non-respondents who decline to answer questions about political party affiliation, either due to privacy concerns or sensitivity about political matters.
Conservative traditionalists with strong religious values who view homosexuality as incompatible with their faith and cultural norms, and would strongly prefer not to have homosexual neighbors.
Moderately conservative individuals who have reservations about homosexuality but are not intensely opposed, and would somewhat dislike having homosexual neighbors while remaining civil.
Pragmatic citizens who focus on practical coexistence and personal character rather than sexual orientation, and would not particularly care about a neighbor's sexual identity.
Socially progressive and tolerant individuals, more common among younger or urban populations, who accept homosexuality and would be comfortable or welcoming toward homosexual neighbors.
Cautious respondents who are uncertain about their views on this sensitive topic or prefer not to express strong opinions due to social pressure or lack of familiarity with the issue.
Rural subsistence farmers with limited infrastructure access who rely on water sources outside their compound, such as communal wells or natural water bodies, as their main household water source.
Semi-urban residents with modest improvements who have water access inside their compound through a shared tap or basic piping system serving multiple households.
Urban or better-off households with modern plumbing who have their main water source piped directly inside their house, reflecting higher income and infrastructure investment.
Transitional households in developing areas who have recently improved their water access to inside the compound but not yet to inside the house itself.
A small minority who are uncertain about how to categorize their water source or prefer not to answer due to sensitivity about their living conditions.

Vaccine-accepting urban/peri-urban residents with better health literacy and access to information. They received COVID-19 vaccination when it became available through government programs or health facilities.

Rural residents with limited health facility access who missed vaccination opportunities despite general willingness. They live far from vaccination centers and lack reliable information about where and when to get vaccinated.

Skeptical or hesitant individuals who doubt vaccine safety or efficacy, or who distrust government health initiatives. They actively chose not to get vaccinated despite awareness of the vaccine program.

Economically vulnerable people who prioritize immediate survival needs over preventive health measures. Given their lack of cash income, they may have deprioritized vaccination or faced barriers affording transportation to clinics.

Individuals with genuine uncertainty about their vaccination status or the details of what they received. They may have received injections but are unsure if they were COVID-19 vaccines or how many doses they got.

Vaccine-hesitant individuals skeptical of government health messaging, particularly given widespread distrust of government institutions evident in corruption concerns. They are unlikely to have received COVID-19 vaccination.

Pragmatic vaccinated individuals who prioritized personal health protection despite general skepticism toward government, viewing vaccination as a practical health measure rather than endorsement of government competence.

Cautious unvaccinated individuals who were uncertain about vaccine safety or effectiveness, neither strongly opposed nor motivated to get vaccinated, reflecting the general 'don't know' and neutral attitudes seen in other responses.

Vaccinated individuals with higher trust in health institutions and scientific consensus, less influenced by broader government distrust, representing those who separated health decisions from political skepticism.

Disengaged individuals with limited access to information or healthcare services who neither received vaccination nor actively refused it, reflecting the small 'don't know' responses seen across other questions.
Urban full-time workers with improved infrastructure access who have water piped inside their homes or compounds, reflecting their higher income and residence in more developed areas.
Rural and semi-urban full-time workers who rely on water sources outside their compounds, such as communal wells or public water points, which is typical for their geographic areas.
Full-time employed individuals in transitional areas with water access inside their compounds but not their homes, representing those with moderate infrastructure development.
A small segment of full-time workers who are uncertain or unwilling to specify their water source location, possibly due to seasonal variation or complex household arrangements.
A minimal group experiencing water access challenges or those who did not respond, representing the smallest portion of this employed demographic.

Religiously observant majority who are comfortable with religious diversity. Having grown up in Malawi's multi-faith communities and valuing harmony, they see people of different religions as acceptable or even welcome neighbors.

Cautious but tolerant individuals who don't strongly prefer one way or another about different religions. They are neutral or mildly positive, reflecting a 'live and let live' attitude despite economic hardships.

Religiously conservative people who somewhat dislike neighbors of different faiths, viewing their own religion as important to community identity. They represent a minority but meaningful perspective in this group.

Strongly religious individuals who actively dislike people of different religions as neighbors, seeing religious boundaries as important. This is a small but present segment reflecting deeper religious conviction.
Uncertain or non-responsive individuals who either don't know their position or refuse to answer, possibly due to social sensitivity around religious topics.
Urban residents with regular internet access who are more informed about health matters and have had direct exposure to COVID-19 cases in their communities or families.
Rural or semi-urban residents with limited internet access who have heard about COVID-19 but have not personally experienced illness or positive cases in their immediate household.
Individuals with moderate internet usage who are somewhat informed about COVID-19 but uncertain whether they or family members had the virus, possibly due to lack of testing access.
Older adults or those with minimal digital engagement who are less aware of COVID-19 details and unlikely to have sought testing, making them uncertain about household exposure.
Health-conscious individuals who actively followed COVID-19 information and took precautions, reducing their likelihood of infection despite living in Côte d'Ivoire.
Daily TV news watchers who rely on television as their primary news source, reflecting the traditional media consumption pattern common in Lesotho.
Regular but not daily TV viewers who watch a few times a week, balancing television news with other occasional information sources.
Occasional TV news consumers who watch a few times a month or less, representing those with limited access or interest in regular television news.
People who never watch television for news, either due to lack of access, preference for other sources, or limited engagement with news media overall.
Those uncertain or unwilling to specify their television news habits, a small segment that may reflect privacy concerns or unclear viewing patterns.
Urban residents with stable employment in the capital or main towns who have reliable electricity access and take it for granted as a basic utility.
Rural or semi-rural residents who have electricity connection but experience occasional outages or unreliable supply, viewing it as an important but sometimes frustrating service.
Lower-income households in remote areas without electricity connection who rely on alternative energy sources like generators or solar panels and face barriers to grid access.
Residents uncertain about their technical connection status or the specifics of their electrical arrangement, who may hesitate to answer definitively.
A small segment unwilling to disclose information about their home utilities or infrastructure for privacy or other reasons.

Urban internet users with regular news exposure: These individuals use the internet daily or several times weekly and stay informed about international affairs through online news sources, making them aware of Japan's development assistance programs to Kenya.

Politically engaged community members: People who frequently discuss political and current affairs with friends and family, keeping them informed about foreign aid and international relations even without heavy internet use.

Rural or less-connected residents with limited information access: Those who rarely use the internet and have minimal exposure to news about international development assistance, leaving them uncertain about Japan's role in Kenya.

Skeptical or distrustful respondents: Individuals experiencing economic hardship who may be cynical about government claims regarding foreign aid or doubt that such assistance actually reaches ordinary Kenyans.
Completely uninformed individuals: People with no exposure to information about Japan or international relations who have genuinely never encountered this topic and cannot form an opinion.
Daily internet users who are digitally connected and rely on the internet for news and information daily
Regular but not daily internet users who access the internet several times a week for various purposes
Occasional internet users who go online a few times a month, often in urban areas with better connectivity
Minimal internet users who rarely or almost never use the internet, relying instead on television and other traditional media
People with no internet access or who have never used the internet, primarily in rural areas with limited infrastructure
Conservative traditionalists with strong religious values who view homosexuality as contrary to their faith and cultural norms, and would strongly dislike having homosexual neighbors.
Pragmatic moderates who may have personal reservations but prioritize peaceful coexistence and would somewhat dislike or not care about homosexual neighbors.
Younger, more cosmopolitan individuals influenced by broader exposure to diverse perspectives who would not care or somewhat like having homosexual neighbors.
Socially progressive community members who actively support inclusion and would strongly like having homosexual neighbors as part of their commitment to diversity.
Cautious individuals uncomfortable with the question or unwilling to express their views openly, who would refuse to answer or express uncertainty.
Deeply distrustful critics who believe the government is doing very badly at fighting corruption, viewing it as systemic and pervasive across institutions.
Moderately critical citizens who think the government is handling corruption fairly badly, acknowledging some efforts but seeing insufficient progress and persistent problems.
Cautiously optimistic or neutral observers who either think the government is doing fairly well at fighting corruption or simply haven't engaged enough with the issue to form a strong opinion.
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who lack sufficient information about government anti-corruption efforts and prefer not to commit to a judgment.
Rare optimists who believe the government is handling corruption very well, though this view is uncommon in the group.
Civically engaged urbanites with higher internet use and education. They actively participate in civic activities including signing petitions as a natural form of political expression.
Religious traditionalists focused on family and community. They may sign petitions on issues aligned with their values, particularly those related to religious or moral concerns.
Passive citizens with limited civic engagement. They rarely sign petitions and see such activities as not relevant to their lives, preferring to stay uninvolved in public affairs.
Skeptical non-participants who distrust institutions and formal civic mechanisms. They view petition-signing as ineffective and prefer to handle problems through personal networks or not at all.
Occasional activists motivated by specific causes. They sign petitions when issues directly affect them or their communities, but lack consistent civic participation habits.
Progressive modernists who strongly support individual autonomy and see choosing not to have children as a perfectly valid life choice deserving of approval.
Moderate liberals who approve of the choice to remain childless as a legitimate personal decision, though without strong conviction.
Pragmatic neutrals who neither approve nor disapprove, viewing childlessness as a personal matter that deserves neither judgment nor endorsement.
Traditional conservatives who mildly disapprove of choosing childlessness, believing parenthood remains an important social norm and life purpose.
Strong traditionalists who firmly disapprove of deliberately remaining childless, viewing it as contrary to natural family values and social responsibility.
Employed wage earners coping financially. These are working-age individuals in regular employment who manage their household income adequately, representing the stable core of the labor force.
Pensioners living on retirement income. Older individuals who have left the workforce and depend primarily on state or occupational pensions, with varying degrees of financial comfort.
Self-employed and small business owners. People running their own enterprises or farms who derive income from self-employment, though this group is relatively small in Bulgaria.

Benefit-dependent households facing financial strain. Individuals relying on unemployment benefits, social assistance, or other state support who struggle significantly with their financial situation.

Multi-source income households with mixed stability. People combining wages with other income sources like investments, family support, or informal work, representing a diverse and less clearly defined group.

Traditional conservatives who strongly disapprove of unmarried cohabitation and non-traditional family structures. They view having children outside marriage as morally wrong and against their values.
Moderate traditionalists who disapprove but are not extreme about it. They have reservations about children born to unmarried couples but acknowledge it happens in modern society.
Pragmatic neutrals who neither approve nor disapprove strongly. They see this as a personal choice and don't judge, though they may not actively choose this path themselves.
Modern progressives who approve of unmarried couples having children together. They view marriage as optional and believe love and commitment matter more than legal status.
Strong progressives who strongly approve of this choice. They actively support non-traditional family structures and see them as equally valid to married families.
Practicing Catholics who maintain strong religious identity and regular engagement with the Church despite secularization trends in Ireland.
Cultural Catholics or lapsed believers who identify with Catholicism as part of their Irish heritage and identity, but don't actively practice.
Secular progressives who have deliberately moved away from religious identification, reflecting Ireland's shift toward secularism and influenced by liberal social views on LGBTQ+ rights.
Agnostics or those uncertain about religion who haven't firmly committed to either religious or secular identity.
Members of other Christian denominations or non-Christian faiths who identify with alternative religious traditions.

Civically disengaged majority who rarely participate in organized activities. They use the internet daily and may pursue professional development, but see organizational work as outside their sphere of concern.
Selective activists who occasionally engage in low-barrier civic actions like petitions or boycotts, but rarely commit to sustained organizational work. They are moderately engaged citizens.
Committed organizational participants who actively work within associations and organizations as part of their civic engagement. They see this as a natural extension of their values.
Professional networkers who engage in organizational work primarily for career advancement and skill-building rather than civic motivation. They view it instrumentally.
Socially isolated individuals with minimal internet use and no participation in any civic or organizational activities. They are largely disconnected from collective action.
Progressive urbanites who strongly support equal rights for same-sex couples, viewing adoption equality as a natural extension of human rights and non-discrimination principles.
Moderate centrists who agree that gay and lesbian couples should have equal adoption rights, seeing this as a matter of fairness and practical child welfare rather than ideology.
Pragmatic fence-sitters who neither strongly agree nor disagree, uncertain about the issue or viewing it as less important than other policy concerns.
Conservative traditionalists who disagree with adoption equality, believing that traditional family structures are preferable for child-rearing despite acknowledging some rights for same-sex couples.
Social conservatives who strongly disagree with adoption rights for same-sex couples, viewing this as contrary to traditional values and what they believe is best for children.
Practical workers focused on immediate job security who see professional development as essential for maintaining employment and advancing in their current roles.
Established workers in stable positions who feel they have sufficient skills and experience, viewing additional training as unnecessary for their current circumstances.
Older workers nearing retirement who have limited motivation to invest time in new skills and see little return on such investments at this stage of their careers.
Career-minded individuals who actively seek out learning opportunities to stay competitive and adapt to changing workplace demands.
Workers in precarious or transitional employment situations who would benefit from training but lack access, time, or resources to pursue it.

Religiously observant traditionalists with conservative social views who prioritize family values and are less likely to engage in consumer activism or boycotts, viewing such actions as outside their sphere of concern.
Secular or non-religious progressives who support LGBTQ+ rights and are more socially conscious, making them more inclined to boycott products based on ethical or political concerns.
Pragmatic working-class individuals with vocational backgrounds who have limited engagement with activism or boycotts, focusing instead on immediate economic concerns and family stability.

Moderate middle-ground citizens who hold mixed views on social issues and may occasionally boycott products for specific reasons (labor practices, environmental concerns) but lack strong ideological commitment to consumer activism.

Union-affiliated or politically engaged workers (24% currently or previously in unions) who are more aware of labor and social justice issues and somewhat more likely to use boycotts as a tool for change.

Progressive urban professionals who strongly reject traditional stigma around homosexuality and would feel no shame whatsoever if a family member were gay, viewing such attitudes as outdated and discriminatory.
Socially liberal but pragmatic workers who disagree with feeling ashamed but may have some residual discomfort, reflecting a live-and-let-live attitude without strong emotional conviction.
Conflicted middle-ground individuals who are uncertain about their feelings on this personal question, neither fully accepting nor rejecting the idea of having a gay family member.
Conservative workers with traditional values who would feel some degree of shame or discomfort if a close family member were gay, though not necessarily extreme rejection.
Strongly traditional individuals who would feel significant shame about having a gay family member, reflecting deeply held conservative or religious beliefs about sexuality.

Pragmatic centrists who feel connected to established parties. These individuals, often with stable employment histories and moderate religious affiliation, see value in identifying with a mainstream political party that represents their economic interests and social values.

Disengaged skeptics wary of all parties. These people, frequently experiencing economic strain and skeptical of institutions, feel that no party adequately represents their concerns and prefer to remain independent from party politics.

Conservative traditionalists aligned with right-wing parties. These individuals, typically more religious and socially traditional, feel a strong affinity for parties that reflect their values on family, religion, and national identity.

Progressive-leaning citizens supporting left or liberal parties. These people, generally more secular and socially liberal, identify with parties that prioritize workers' rights, social tolerance, and progressive policies.

Apathetic non-voters disconnected from politics. These individuals, often economically vulnerable and distrustful of the political system, see little difference between parties and feel politics is irrelevant to their lives.

Politically engaged professionals who actively participate in civic life through petitions and organizational work, and view trade unions as important institutions for worker representation and collective action.
Moderately active citizens who occasionally sign petitions and support social participation, and see trade union membership as a reasonable way to protect worker interests, though not a priority.
Pragmatic workers with past union experience who valued the protections and solidarity unions provided during their working years, but are no longer actively involved.

Independent-minded individuals who prefer to handle their own affairs without organizational membership, viewing trade unions as less relevant to their personal circumstances or ideological preferences.
Younger or more individualistic women who have limited exposure to union culture, work in sectors without strong union presence, or prioritize flexibility over collective membership structures.

Digitally disconnected traditionalists who rarely use the internet and have minimal civic engagement. They are unlikely to sign petitions as they are largely disconnected from modern activism channels.

Occasional internet users with low civic participation who view petition-signing as not particularly relevant to their lives. They represent the passive majority who don't actively engage in civic activities.

Regular internet users with moderate civic interest who may occasionally sign petitions when they encounter causes they care about. They represent the digitally engaged but selectively active segment.
Daily internet users with stronger civic values who actively support causes through petitions and other means. They are more likely to sign petitions as part of their regular online activities.

Socially conscious activists who regularly engage in civic activities including petition-signing, boycotts, and organizational work. Though small in number, they represent the most engaged segment of this retired population.
Non-unionized private sector workers and self-employed individuals who have never joined a union, viewing them as unnecessary or preferring individual negotiation.
Currently active union members, primarily in public sector or traditional industries, who value collective bargaining and worker protections.
Former union members who were organized earlier in their careers but have since left the workforce, changed sectors, or opted out as circumstances changed.
Young urban professionals in service or knowledge economy sectors who are skeptical of traditional unions and see them as outdated or irrelevant to their work.
Politically engaged citizens with strong ideological views about unions, either as essential protectors of workers' rights or as obstacles to economic flexibility.
Secular-minded individuals who have moved away from religious practice and identity, viewing religion as less relevant to modern Norwegian life.
Culturally Christian Norwegians who identify with the Lutheran tradition as part of their cultural heritage and national identity, even if not actively practicing.
Actively religious believers who maintain regular faith practice and consider their religious denomination an important part of their personal identity.
Pragmatic individuals who are nominally registered with a church but don't strongly identify with religion in their daily lives.
Members of minority religious communities (Muslim, Buddhist, Hindu, etc.) who actively identify with their faith tradition.

Socially disengaged majority: People with low civic participation who rarely sign petitions, boycott products, or join organizations. They view organizational work as something others do, not part of their routine.

Religiously-grounded community members: Highly religious Poles (91% identify with religion) who may participate in church or faith-based organizations but are selective about secular civic engagement.

Socially progressive activists: Younger, more educated individuals who support LGBTQ+ rights (61% agree gays should live freely) and engage in multiple forms of civic action including organizational work.

Working-class organizers: People from families where mothers worked as employees (45%) who have practical experience with organizational structures and may participate in workplace or trade union organizations.
Self-employed/entrepreneurial types: Those from self-employed family backgrounds (26%) who may view organizational participation through a business or professional lens rather than activism.
Retired professionals who remain intellectually engaged and regularly pursue learning opportunities through courses and conferences to stay current in their fields or explore new interests.
Moderately active seniors who occasionally attend lectures or take courses when something specific interests them, but don't make continuous learning a regular habit.
Digitally connected retirees who use the internet daily and engage with online learning resources, webinars, and virtual courses as their primary mode of skill development.
Traditionally-oriented older adults with limited internet use who rarely participate in formal courses or conferences, preferring informal knowledge-sharing within their communities.
Disengaged seniors with minimal internet access or interest in formal learning, who have largely stepped away from professional development and structured educational activities.
Politically disengaged majority who rarely participate in civic activities. They don't sign petitions and see little point in such symbolic gestures.
Occasional civic participants with moderate interest in social issues. They might sign a petition if it concerns something they care about, but it's not a regular habit.
Active citizens who regularly engage in various forms of political expression including petitions. They view petition-signing as a legitimate way to voice concerns.
Selective activists focused on specific causes like consumer ethics or environmental protection. They may sign petitions aligned with their particular values.
Highly engaged civic participants who combine multiple forms of activism including petitions, boycotts, and organizational work. They see petition-signing as part of broader civic engagement.

Non-unionized private sector workers who have never joined a union, viewing them as unnecessary or preferring individual employment arrangements. They represent the largest segment of Swiss workers in 2016.
Currently active union members, primarily in public sector or traditionally unionized industries, who see unions as important for protecting worker rights and maintaining labor standards.
Former union members who were previously involved but have since left, either due to job changes, career progression, or declining belief in union relevance to their current situation.

Skilled tradespeople and professionals in regulated sectors who maintain union membership as a practical necessity for their profession, viewing it as standard practice rather than ideological commitment.
Young workers and recent immigrants to Switzerland who are unfamiliar with union culture or skeptical of traditional labor organizations, preferring flexible work arrangements.

Engaged workers with strong union ties. These individuals are currently active union members who value collective worker representation and see unions as essential for protecting labor rights and workplace conditions.

Former union members who moved on. These people had union experience earlier in their careers but are no longer members, either due to job changes, career progression, or reduced perceived need for union representation.

Skeptical non-members in stable employment. These individuals have never joined unions and don't see the need, typically working in sectors or positions where they feel adequately protected or where union culture is weak.
Ideologically opposed to unions. A smaller segment that actively rejects union membership on principle, viewing unions as outdated, bureaucratic, or contrary to individual merit-based advancement.

Unaware or indifferent non-members. These people have simply never engaged with the question of union membership, either because unions aren't present in their workplace or because they haven't considered it relevant to their situation.

Active professionals engaged in continuous learning. These are typically younger, highly educated individuals who use the internet daily and actively seek professional development through courses and conferences to advance their careers.

Moderately engaged workers with selective professional development. They pursue training occasionally when they see clear career benefits, but don't make it a regular habit, balancing work demands with other life priorities.

Established workers with stable positions. These individuals, often older or in secure roles, see less need for formal professional development and rely on experience rather than structured learning to maintain their work competence.

Digitally disconnected or retired individuals. With limited internet use and often outside the active workforce, they have minimal engagement with professional development opportunities and see little relevance to their current situation.

Self-directed learners who prefer informal development. These people develop skills through work experience, informal networks, and self-study rather than formal courses or conferences, viewing structured professional development as unnecessary.

Religiously observant traditionalists with conservative social views who prioritize family and community values. They are unlikely to engage in product boycotts as they tend to focus on personal and religious obligations rather than activism.
Secular or non-religious progressives who support LGBTQ+ rights and equality. They are more inclined to boycott products as part of their broader commitment to social justice and ethical consumption.

Moderate middle-ground individuals who hold mixed views on social issues and are neither strongly religious nor strongly secular. They occasionally engage in boycotts when issues directly affect them or their families.

Working-class individuals with union experience or family history of labor activism who view boycotts as a legitimate tool for worker and consumer rights. They are moderately likely to participate in boycotts.

Apolitical or disengaged citizens who are not particularly active in social or political causes. They rarely engage in boycotts due to lack of awareness or motivation to participate in such activities.
Progressive urbanites and younger people who strongly support individual choice and see childlessness as a valid life path; they view reproductive autonomy as a fundamental right.
Moderate pragmatists who accept that not having children is a reasonable personal choice, though they may personally value parenthood; they are comfortable with diverse life paths.
Traditionalists influenced by Catholic values who believe parenthood is an important social duty and view childlessness with some disapproval, though they tolerate it as a personal decision.
Conservative Catholics and family-focused individuals who disapprove of choosing childlessness, seeing it as selfish or contrary to natural purpose and traditional family values.
Ambivalent middle-grounders who neither approve nor disapprove, uncertain about the morality of the choice or simply indifferent to others' reproductive decisions.
Traditional conservatives who disapprove of non-marital relationships and childbearing. They view having children outside marriage as morally wrong and contrary to family values.

Cautious moderates who are uncertain about non-marital child-rearing but lean slightly negative. They neither fully approve nor disapprove, reflecting ambivalence about departing from traditional norms.

Pragmatic progressives who approve of having children with an unmarried partner they live with. They see cohabitation and child-rearing as acceptable alternatives to marriage, valuing commitment over legal status.

Strong liberals who strongly approve of non-marital families. They view marriage as unnecessary for legitimate family formation and believe individuals should be free to structure their relationships as they choose.

Lived-experience pragmatists who have personally cohabited without marriage and approve of this lifestyle for child-rearing. Their acceptance is grounded in their own experience of successful non-marital partnerships.
Traditional family values advocates who believe having children is a fundamental life purpose and disapprove of choosing childlessness as selfish or unnatural.
Moderate traditionalists who have some reservations about childlessness but recognize it as a personal choice, leaning toward disapproval but not strongly.
Pragmatic middle-grounders who neither approve nor disapprove, viewing childlessness as a legitimate personal decision without strong moral judgment either way.
Modern-minded approvers who respect individual autonomy and believe people should be free to choose whether or not to have children based on their own circumstances.
Strong individualists who strongly approve of the right to remain childless, viewing it as an important expression of personal freedom and self-determination.
Stable wage earners in secure employment with adequate household income. They view their financial situation as manageable and feel they are coping well on their present income.
Self-employed professionals and small business owners with variable but generally sufficient income. They typically cope on their present income, though some experience fluctuations.
Pensioners and older adults living on fixed retirement income. Most feel they are coping adequately, though some experience financial strain due to limited income sources.

Lower-income households including those on social benefits or with precarious employment. They find it difficult or very difficult to manage on their present income and face genuine financial hardship.
Young adults or households in transition between jobs or life stages. They experience variable financial comfort, ranging from coping to finding it difficult depending on their current circumstances.

Conservative nationalists with traditional values. They strongly oppose immigration from poorer countries, viewing it as a threat to Russian identity, jobs, and social stability. They align with the group's demonstrated skepticism toward social change and openness to diversity.

Pragmatic moderates focused on economic stability. They would allow only a few immigrants, seeing some controlled immigration as potentially beneficial for labor needs but wanting strict limits to protect existing living standards and social cohesion.

Socially liberal professionals with higher education and international exposure. They support allowing some immigration based on humanitarian concerns and economic benefits, though they remain a minority given the group's overall conservative leanings on social issues.

Economically anxious working-class individuals concerned about competition for jobs and resources. They oppose significant immigration, preferring to allow none or only a few, reflecting their precarious economic position despite the group's overall financial comfort.

Cosmopolitan internationalists with progressive views. They support allowing many immigrants based on universal humanitarian principles, though they represent a very small segment given the group's demonstrated strong agreement with traditional values and skepticism of social change.

Urban professionals with employed mothers (40-45% of group). These are typically younger, well-educated Estonians who grew up in cities where their mothers worked as employees in the formal economy, reflecting the Soviet-era norm of female workforce participation.

Post-Soviet working-class individuals whose mothers were employees (25-30% of group). They come from families where both parents worked in state enterprises or public sector jobs, a common pattern in Soviet Estonia that continued into the 1990s-2000s.

Rural and small-town residents whose mothers were self-employed or in informal work (15-18% of group). These individuals grew up in less urbanized areas where their mothers engaged in small business, farming-related work, or informal economic activities.

Those from non-traditional family structures (8-10% of group). This includes people whose mothers were not working due to disability, early retirement, or family circumstances, or who experienced maternal absence or death.

Younger generation with limited memory or knowledge (3-5% of group). These are individuals too young to clearly remember their mother's employment status at age 14, or who may not have reliable information about their family background.

Restrictive nationalists (primarily older, traditional values). They believe Hungary should allow none or very few immigrants from poorer countries, viewing immigration as a threat to national identity and resources.
Cautious moderates (middle-aged, economically stable). They support allowing some immigration but with careful controls, seeing both economic concerns and humanitarian considerations as important.

Selective pragmatists (younger, urban professionals). They would allow some to come and live in Hungary, believing in selective immigration based on skills and economic needs rather than blanket restrictions.
Liberal humanitarians (educated, socially progressive). They support allowing many people from poorer countries to immigrate, viewing this as a moral obligation and seeing diversity as beneficial.

Ambivalent undecideds (less politically engaged). They are uncertain about immigration policy, lacking strong convictions either way and potentially swayed by economic circumstances or political messaging.

Pragmatic non-participants: Working-class individuals focused on immediate economic concerns who see boycotts as ineffective or a luxury they cannot afford; they prioritize putting food on the table over consumer activism.

Skeptical traditionalists: People with conservative social views who are suspicious of boycott movements, viewing them as politically motivated campaigns by elites that don't reflect ordinary people's real concerns.

Selective activists: Individuals who occasionally boycott products for practical reasons (quality, price, local preference) but don't see themselves as part of organized consumer movements or social campaigns.

Engaged progressives: Younger or more educated members of the group who support boycotts as a tool for social and environmental change, though they may face economic constraints that limit their participation.
Passive disengaged: People with low trust in institutions and little faith that individual actions like boycotts create meaningful change, so they simply don't participate.
Politically disengaged traditionalists who rarely participate in civic activities. They see petition-signing as unnecessary activism and prefer to let established institutions handle problems.
Moderate civic participants who occasionally sign petitions on issues they care about, viewing it as a reasonable way to express concerns without major commitment.
Active social advocates who regularly sign petitions as part of their broader engagement in civil society and consumer activism.
Skeptical pragmatists who doubt petitions are effective and believe direct action or political engagement through established channels is more worthwhile.
Former union members and organizational activists who have stepped back from civic engagement in recent years and now rarely participate in petition campaigns.

Traditional conservatives who believe in strict social norms and traditional family values. They disapprove of homosexuality on moral or religious grounds and believe gay people should conform to societal expectations rather than live freely as they wish.

Moderate traditionalists who are uncomfortable with homosexuality but recognize individual autonomy to some degree. They may tolerate gay people living their lives but with reservations, reflecting ambivalence between personal discomfort and acceptance of freedom.

Pragmatic neutrals who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of gay lifestyles. They believe people should be free to live as they wish but don't feel strongly about it, maintaining a live-and-let-live attitude without active support.

Liberal supporters who believe gay men and lesbians should absolutely be free to live their own lives without restriction. They actively support equal freedom and reject discrimination based on sexual orientation.
Passionate advocates who strongly agree that gay people deserve complete freedom to live as they wish. They view this as a fundamental human right and actively support LGBTQ+ equality and dignity.

Orthodox believers who maintain strong religious identity and practice. For them, religion is a central part of their cultural and personal identity, especially given Russia's Orthodox Christian heritage.
Non-religious secular individuals who have deliberately rejected religious affiliation and see themselves as atheist or agnostic. They view religion as unnecessary for a meaningful life.

Culturally religious but non-practicing people who identify with Orthodoxy as part of their Russian heritage rather than active faith. They see religion more as cultural tradition than personal conviction.
Indifferent or uncertain individuals who haven't given much thought to religious identity and may fluctuate in their self-identification. They are neither committed believers nor strong atheists.
Members of minority faiths (Islam, Catholicism, Protestantism, Judaism) who identify with their specific religious denomination. They represent a small but distinct segment of the population.
Practicing Catholics from traditional farming families who maintain strong religious identity and attend church regularly as part of their community and cultural heritage.
Secular or lapsed Catholics who were raised in the faith but no longer practice or identify strongly with religion in their daily lives.
Non-religious individuals who actively reject religious identification and see themselves as atheist or agnostic.
Members of other Christian denominations (Protestant, Church of Ireland) who maintain their distinct religious identity within the Irish countryside.
Individuals from immigrant backgrounds or those who practice non-Christian religions, representing growing religious diversity in rural Ireland.
Professionally engaged workers in stable careers who regularly invest in skill development through courses and conferences to advance their expertise and stay competitive.
Employed individuals in routine or established roles who feel their current skills are sufficient and see little need for formal professional development activities.
Self-employed entrepreneurs and business owners who actively pursue training and knowledge-building as essential to maintaining and growing their enterprises.
Workers with limited access to or awareness of professional development opportunities, or those in precarious employment situations where such courses are not readily available or affordable.
Individuals approaching retirement or in later career stages who have less motivation to pursue new training and feel established enough in their roles.
Progressive-minded urban professionals who strongly support equal rights for LGBTQ+ couples, viewing adoption equality as a matter of basic fairness and non-discrimination.
Socially liberal but cautious moderates who agree that gay and lesbian couples should have adoption rights, though they may have some reservations about implementation details.
Pragmatic centrists who are neutral on the issue, either genuinely undecided about whether adoption rights should be equal or uncomfortable taking a strong stance either way.

Conservative traditionalists who believe that traditional family structures are preferable and disagree with granting equal adoption rights to same-sex couples, though not necessarily with strong intensity.
Strong social conservatives who firmly oppose equal adoption rights for gay and lesbian couples based on traditional or religious values about family structure.
Secular progressives who have rejected religious affiliation entirely, viewing religion as incompatible with modern, liberal values. They represent the largest segment of this young Belgian cohort.
Cultural Catholics or nominal believers who maintain a loose connection to their religious heritage for family or cultural reasons, even if they don't actively practice.
Committed religious individuals who actively identify with their faith community, whether Catholic, Protestant, or another denomination, and see religion as important to their identity.
Agnostics or spiritual-but-not-religious people who are uncertain about religious claims but haven't completely rejected the possibility of spirituality or religious belonging.

Recent immigrants or members of minority faith communities (Muslim, Jewish, Orthodox Christian, etc.) who maintain strong religious identification distinct from Belgium's traditional Christian heritage.
Pragmatic moderates who see cohabitation as a normal, acceptable lifestyle choice. They neither strongly approve nor disapprove, viewing it as a personal decision that doesn't require moral judgment.
Progressive acceptors who actively approve of cohabitation without marriage, seeing it as a legitimate alternative to traditional marriage that reflects modern values and personal freedom.
Traditional skeptics who disapprove of cohabitation without marriage, preferring the institution of marriage and viewing unmarried cohabitation as morally questionable or socially problematic.
Strongly traditional conservatives who strongly disapprove of cohabitation without marriage on moral or religious grounds, viewing it as a violation of proper social norms.
Enthusiastic progressives who strongly approve of cohabitation, actively endorsing it as a positive expression of personal autonomy and modern relationship freedom.
Progressive urbanites and younger villagers with strong liberal values who firmly reject any shame about LGBTQ+ family members, viewing such attitudes as outdated and discriminatory.

Socially tolerant mainstream villagers who accept LGBTQ+ people's right to live freely but feel some personal discomfort or ambivalence about having a gay family member, reflecting traditional social norms.
Traditional Catholics and religious conservatives who hold conventional family values and would experience genuine shame or distress if a close family member were gay, though they may not be hostile.
Conflicted middle-ground residents who neither strongly embrace nor reject the idea, uncertain about their own feelings and reflecting broader social change in Belgian villages.
Strongly traditional or religiously fundamentalist villagers who view homosexuality as morally wrong and would feel significant shame, representing the most conservative segment.
Conservative nationalists with restrictive views on immigration. They prioritize national resources and cultural preservation, favoring minimal immigration from poorer countries outside Europe.
Pragmatic moderates who accept some immigration but with careful limits. They believe in controlled, selective immigration that balances humanitarian concerns with practical economic considerations.

Socially liberal cosmopolitans with more open attitudes toward immigration. They support allowing a reasonable number of people from poorer countries, viewing it as both a moral and practical responsibility.
Conflicted middle-grounders uncertain about immigration policy. They neither strongly support nor oppose immigration, reflecting ambivalence about Hungary's role in addressing global poverty.
Humanitarian advocates for generous immigration policies. They believe Hungary should allow many people from poorer countries, prioritizing human rights and compassion over restrictive nationalism.

Daily digital natives: Young professionals and engaged citizens who use the internet every day across multiple devices for work, social connection, and civic participation. They are comfortable online and represent the digitally integrated segment of Swedish small-town society.

Regular weekday users: Working-age adults who use the internet most days, primarily for work-related tasks and some personal use, but may not be constantly connected. They represent the mainstream employed population.

Moderate occasional users: Older adults or those less professionally dependent on digital tools who use the internet a few times a week for specific purposes like email, news, or banking. They are digitally literate but not daily users.

Minimal users: Elderly residents or those with limited digital engagement who only occasionally use the internet, perhaps for essential services or with family assistance. They represent the digitally disconnected minority.
Non-users: A small segment, primarily older residents, who never use the internet and rely on traditional communication and information methods.
Stable wage earners in secure employment who have adapted to village life and manage their household budget reasonably well, feeling they are coping adequately with their income.
Older residents living on pensions who have modest but predictable income and have learned to live within their means over decades, generally coping with their financial situation.
Self-employed workers and small business owners in the village whose income fluctuates seasonally, experiencing periods where household finances become difficult to manage.
Younger families or those with irregular employment who struggle significantly with household expenses and feel financial strain is a constant reality of their lives.

Agricultural workers or those dependent on farming-related income whose livelihoods are vulnerable to market conditions and weather, making their financial situation precarious and often very difficult.

Progressive liberals who strongly reject traditional stigma around homosexuality. They would firmly disagree with feeling ashamed of a gay family member, viewing such feelings as discriminatory and contrary to personal freedom.

Socially liberal but pragmatic individuals who disagree with the statement but may have some residual discomfort. They support LGBTQ+ rights intellectually and would not feel ashamed, though they might acknowledge complex family dynamics.

Moderates who are genuinely uncertain about their feelings on this deeply personal question. They neither strongly endorse nor reject the idea of feeling ashamed, reflecting ambivalence about family acceptance.
Traditional conservatives who would feel some degree of shame or discomfort with a gay family member, viewing homosexuality through a more conventional moral or religious lens.
Strong traditionalists who would agree they would feel ashamed, reflecting deeply held conservative or religious values that view homosexuality as problematic.

Wage earners coping financially. These are employed individuals who rely on regular salaries to support their households and manage to get by on their current income, representing the economic backbone of the group.
Pensioners with modest means. Older individuals living primarily on pensions who face financial constraints but have adapted to their fixed income situation.
Self-employed and small business owners. People running their own enterprises or farms who derive income from self-employment, though this group is relatively smaller within the demographic.

Financially struggling households. Individuals and families experiencing significant difficulty on their present income, relying on various social benefits or unemployment support to supplement inadequate earnings.

Those with investment or other income sources. A small minority with income from savings, investments, or other non-traditional sources who may have more financial stability than wage-dependent peers.
Religiously engaged civic participants who believe in collective action and have signed petitions as a way to advocate for causes they care about, often motivated by faith-based values.
Socially liberal, moderately active older adults who support progressive causes like LGBTQ+ rights and occasionally engage in civic actions like petition signing when issues align with their values.
Traditional, religiously observant individuals who are less inclined toward activism and consumer boycotts, viewing petition signing as unnecessary or ineffective for creating change.
Politically disengaged older adults who rarely participate in any form of civic activism, including petition signing, preferring to focus on personal and family matters.
Selective activists who engage in specific causes they feel strongly about but are inconsistent in their participation across different forms of civic engagement.
Progressive urbanites who embrace modern family structures. They strongly approve of unmarried cohabitation and childbearing, viewing these as personal choices free from traditional constraints.

Pragmatic moderates who accept non-traditional family arrangements without strong feelings either way. They approve or remain neutral on unmarried partners having children, seeing it as a normal contemporary reality.

Traditional conservatives who disapprove of children born outside marriage. They believe in formal marriage as the proper foundation for family and child-rearing, though they may tolerate cohabitation itself.

Conflicted middle-grounders uncertain about unmarried childbearing specifically. They may accept cohabitation but have reservations about children without marriage, reflecting lingering traditional values mixed with modern acceptance.
Strict traditionalists who strongly disapprove of any family arrangement outside marriage. They view unmarried childbearing as morally problematic and contrary to proper family values.
Career-focused professionals and skilled workers who regularly invest in continuous learning and professional development to advance their careers and stay competitive in their fields.
Established workers with stable employment who feel their skills are sufficient for their current roles and see little need for additional training or professional development.
Self-employed individuals and entrepreneurs who actively pursue courses and conferences to develop business skills, market knowledge, and professional networks essential for their ventures.
Younger workers and those early in their careers who occasionally attend training or lectures when required by employers or when seeking to transition to new roles.
Workers in manual or routine occupations with limited access to or perceived need for formal professional development opportunities beyond their current job requirements.

Stable wage earners coping financially. These are employed individuals who rely on regular salaries and manage their household budgets adequately, representing the backbone of the Bulgarian workforce in 2020.
Pensioners with modest means. Older adults living primarily on pensions who experience some financial strain but have accepted their economic situation as part of retirement.
Self-employed and small business owners. Entrepreneurs and self-employed individuals whose income is less stable but who maintain moderate financial security through their own enterprises.

Benefit-dependent households facing hardship. People relying on social benefits, unemployment support, or other grants who struggle significantly with their financial situation and experience real economic difficulty.
Multi-income households with mixed sources. Families combining wages with other income sources like farming, investments, or supplementary benefits, creating more complex financial situations.
Pragmatic liberals who see cohabitation and non-traditional family structures as normal and acceptable modern choices. They approve of unmarried couples having children together.
Tolerant moderates who don't strongly object to unmarried couples having children but feel somewhat uncertain about it. They neither strongly approve nor disapprove.
Cautious traditionalists who have reservations about children born outside marriage but aren't strongly opposed. They lean toward disapproval but acknowledge it happens.
Secular skeptics indifferent to marital status as a moral issue, viewing it as a practical rather than ethical matter. They see no reason to disapprove of unmarried parents.
Conservative disapprovers who believe marriage should precede childbearing and view unmarried parenthood as problematic, though they represent a small minority in this secular Czech group.
Digitally engaged, socially conscious urbanites who use the internet daily and are aware of ethical consumption issues; they actively boycott products for moral or environmental reasons.
Regular internet users with moderate social awareness who occasionally consider boycotts but don't make it a regular practice due to convenience or lack of strong conviction.
Older or less digitally connected Italians who use the internet infrequently and have limited exposure to boycott campaigns; they rarely engage in product boycotts.
Pragmatic consumers focused on price and availability rather than ethical considerations; they are skeptical of boycott effectiveness and don't participate.
Politically disengaged individuals who view boycotts as ineffective or irrelevant to their lives; they see consumer activism as performative.
Strong party identifiers with clear political allegiances, typically aligned with major parties like Fianna Fáil or Fine Gael. They feel a definite sense of belonging to their chosen party.
Moderate party supporters who lean toward a particular party but don't feel strongly attached to it. They might consider alternatives depending on circumstances.
Independent-minded voters who deliberately avoid identifying with any single party, preferring to evaluate candidates and policies on individual merit each election.
Disengaged or apathetic voters who haven't thought much about party affiliation or don't see meaningful differences between parties worth committing to.
Ideologically driven voters who feel closer to smaller or niche parties (like Sinn Féin, Greens, or independents) that better represent their specific values.
Socially disengaged individuals who rarely participate in civic activities of any kind. They don't work in organizations or associations and see such involvement as not relevant to their lives.
