Agnostic or uncertain individuals who genuinely don't know whether God exists or cares about individuals, finding the question unanswerable.
Spiritual but non-religious people who believe in some form of higher power or cosmic force but not necessarily a personal God concerned with individuals.
Theistic believers who affirm that God exists and takes a personal interest in human beings, though they may vary in conviction strength.
Secular skeptics who reject belief in God entirely and see no evidence for divine existence. They view life as meaningful through human connection and achievement rather than religious faith.
Agnostic doubters uncertain about God's existence and unconvinced that the question can be resolved. They maintain an open but skeptical stance, neither committing to belief nor disbelief.

Spiritual but not religious believers who acknowledge a Higher Power or transcendent force without accepting traditional personal God concepts. They find meaning in spirituality while maintaining intellectual distance from organized religion.
Conflicted believers who experience fluctuating faith, sometimes believing in God and sometimes doubting. Their religious conviction is genuine but unstable, reflecting ongoing internal struggle.

Committed believers with strong, unwavering faith in God's existence and personal concern for humanity. They integrate religious belief deeply into their worldview and find life's meaning through their relationship with God.
Healthy individuals with minimal healthcare needs who rarely require medical treatment and thus have not experienced waiting list issues.
Regular healthcare users with manageable conditions who access treatment without significant delays, viewing the Swiss healthcare system as generally responsive.
Patients with chronic or ongoing conditions who have experienced frustrating delays in accessing needed treatments, particularly for specialist care or elective procedures.
Pragmatic individuals who acknowledge occasional waiting times but view them as an acceptable trade-off for Switzerland's universal healthcare coverage and quality standards.
Skeptical or disengaged respondents uncertain about their healthcare experiences or unwilling to clearly categorize their situation regarding treatment access.
Secular skeptics who reject belief in God entirely and see no evidence for divine existence. They represent the substantial non-religious segment of Israeli society.
Agnostic pragmatists who are genuinely uncertain about God's existence and believe the question may be unknowable. They are comfortable with ambiguity on metaphysical questions.
Spiritual but not religious believers who reject a personal God but acknowledge some kind of higher power or cosmic force. They seek meaning beyond strict materialism without traditional theism.
Doubtful believers who experience fluctuating faith, sometimes believing in God and sometimes doubting, reflecting an internal struggle between skepticism and spiritual inclination.
Committed theists with strong, unwavering belief in God's existence, though some may have minor doubts. They form the core of the religiously observant population in Israel.
Secular skeptics who reject religious concepts. They don't believe in hell and see it as a cultural myth with no basis in reality.
Agnostic pragmatists uncertain about supernatural matters. They're unsure whether hell exists and prefer not to commit to a definitive answer.
Moderate believers with some religious inclination. They think hell probably exists as part of a broader religious framework, though without strong conviction.
Committed religious believers who accept hell as real doctrine. They definitely believe in hell as part of their faith tradition.
Inconsistent believers who hold mixed views on religious concepts. They might believe in some aspects like life after death but remain doubtful about hell specifically.

Conservative traditionalists who view abortion as morally wrong in most circumstances, including cases of financial hardship, seeing it as incompatible with their traditional values despite being non-religious.
Pragmatic moderates who believe abortion is sometimes justified when families face severe economic hardship, viewing the welfare of existing family members as a legitimate consideration.
Secular progressives who see abortion as a woman's right and not wrong when she cannot afford more children, prioritizing reproductive autonomy and practical life circumstances.
Conflicted individuals who are genuinely uncertain about abortion in cases of poverty, torn between sympathy for difficult circumstances and lingering moral reservations.
Disengaged respondents who prefer not to take a stance on this sensitive issue and select the 'can't choose' option.
Healthy individuals with minimal healthcare needs who rarely require medical treatment and therefore have not experienced waiting list issues.
People with occasional healthcare needs who accessed treatment without significant delays, either through private healthcare or timely public system access.
Individuals with chronic or regular healthcare needs who have experienced delays in the public healthcare system due to long waiting lists.
People with urgent or serious health conditions who managed to bypass long waiting lists through private healthcare options or prioritized treatment.
Those uncertain about their healthcare experiences or unfamiliar with how to navigate the system, unable to clearly categorize their situation.

Solidly middle-class suburban professionals who feel economically secure and socially established in their communities. They see themselves as firmly in the middle-to-upper-middle of society's hierarchy, typically placing themselves around 6-7 on the scale.

Working-class or lower-middle-class residents who experience economic precarity and feel somewhat disadvantaged compared to wealthier urban center dwellers. They tend to place themselves in the lower-middle range, around 4-5, reflecting their sense of being below average in societal position.

Affluent suburban dwellers with strong economic security and social confidence who view themselves as clearly above average in society's hierarchy. They consistently place themselves in the upper range, typically 7-8 or higher.

Individuals with more egalitarian or critical perspectives on social hierarchies who are skeptical of ranking themselves on such scales, viewing the concept itself as problematic. They may place themselves in the middle (5) as a form of resistance to the hierarchy framework.

Younger or more precarious residents uncertain about their long-term position in society, experiencing economic volatility or career instability. They express uncertainty about where they belong, often selecting lower-middle positions (3-4) due to anxiety about their future prospects.
Environmentally conscious recyclers who make a consistent effort to sort recyclables as part of their regular routine and view it as an important personal responsibility.
Casual recyclers who participate in recycling sometimes when it's convenient, but don't make a special effort or maintain consistent habits.
Inconsistent participants who recycle occasionally but lack strong motivation, often forgetting or deprioritizing the effort required.
Non-recyclers who never make an effort to sort recyclables, either due to lack of access, low environmental concern, or simple indifference.
Ideologically motivated recyclers who combine environmental values with practical action, viewing recycling as aligned with their broader sustainability beliefs.
Non-religious secularists (53% of group) who don't follow any religion and have little engagement with religious texts; they would answer 'No' as scripture reading is not part of their worldview.
Believers with faith but limited scripture engagement (28% of group) who believe in God and consider themselves religious, yet rarely read scriptures outside of worship services; they answer 'No'.

Occasional scripture readers (12% of group) who identify as religious or spiritual and have read or listened to religious texts in the past year out of personal interest or practice; they answer 'Yes'.

Agnostics and spiritual seekers (8% of group) who are uncertain about God or believe in a higher power but not organized religion, and may occasionally explore various spiritual texts; they answer 'Yes' or 'No' depending on their curiosity.
Uncertain or non-committal respondents (4% of group) who are unclear about their religious identity or scripture engagement habits; they answer 'Don't know'.

Environmentally Committed Activists: Upper-middle-class professionals who consistently recycle, read environmental literature, and actively engage in environmental advocacy through petitions and other means. They see signing environmental petitions as a natural extension of their values and lifestyle.

Conscientious but Passive Environmentalists: Well-educated individuals who prioritize recycling and environmental concerns in their personal habits but rarely take public action like signing petitions. They believe individual responsibility is more important than collective political action.

Selective Issue Advocates: Affluent citizens who care about specific environmental causes that directly affect them (clean water, local pollution) and will sign petitions on those particular issues, but don't engage broadly with environmental activism.

Disengaged but Aware: Upper-middle-class individuals who acknowledge environmental concerns and may recycle occasionally, but feel disconnected from activism and skeptical that petitions create meaningful change. They rarely sign environmental petitions.

Dismissive Skeptics: Affluent individuals who view environmental activism as performative or exaggerated, prioritize economic concerns over environmental ones, and have not signed environmental petitions despite their social class position.
Mainstream public system users: Middle-class French citizens satisfied with the national health insurance system (Sécurité Sociale), viewing it as adequate and comprehensive for their needs.
Dual coverage pragmatists: Middle-class professionals who maintain both public national insurance and private complementary insurance to cover gaps and reduce out-of-pocket costs.
Private insurance preferrers: Wealthier individuals or those with employer benefits who rely primarily on private insurance while maintaining minimal public coverage.
Uninsured or underinsured: Lower-income individuals who either lack adequate coverage or are unaware of their insurance status due to administrative complexity.
Uncertain navigators: People confused about their coverage type or the distinctions between public, private, and complementary insurance options available to them.
Committed Catholic believers who actively practice their faith and believe in a personal God deeply involved in human affairs. They see God's providence as central to their worldview.

Cultural Catholics who follow the religion but are not particularly spiritual or engaged; they are skeptical about God's personal involvement in individual lives and tend toward agnosticism on this question.
Secular or non-religious individuals who reject the premise of a personal God entirely, viewing such beliefs as unfounded regardless of their cultural Catholic background.
Spiritual but non-dogmatic people who believe in some higher power or transcendence but are uncertain whether it takes the form of a personal God concerned with individuals.
Undecided or conflicted individuals who genuinely cannot choose between belief and disbelief, reflecting broader uncertainty about religious claims in this population.
Environmentally conscious activists who regularly recycle and engage in environmental causes, viewing petition-signing as a natural extension of their ecological commitment.
Moderately engaged villagers who recycle sometimes and care about environmental issues but haven't taken the step to sign petitions due to limited awareness or access to such opportunities.
Practical-minded residents focused on daily survival and family welfare in rural settings, with limited interest in or exposure to environmental activism despite some recycling habits.
Skeptical or disengaged individuals who see environmental petitions as ineffective or irrelevant to their lives, preferring to focus on immediate local concerns.
Older or more traditional villagers with strong religious faith and conservative values who may view environmental activism with indifference or suspicion as a modern urban concern.
Healthy pragmatists with minimal healthcare needs who rarely encounter waiting lists because they don't require frequent medical treatment.
Regular healthcare users who navigate the Swiss system competently and generally receive timely treatment through established channels, accepting occasional minor delays as normal.
Frustrated patients who have experienced genuine delays in accessing needed medical care and view Switzerland's waiting lists as a real problem affecting their health.
Cautious skeptics who worry about potential waiting list issues but haven't personally experienced significant delays, remaining uncertain about the true extent of the problem.
Disengaged respondents who find the question unclear or lack sufficient healthcare experience to answer meaningfully, including those with private insurance who perceive different access patterns.

Pragmatic workers concerned about economic competition. They see immigrants as potentially harmful to job availability and wages for local workers, viewing immigration through a lens of economic self-interest and resource scarcity.
Tradition-focused community members who prefer social stability. They believe immigrants disrupt established customs and social cohesion, and worry about cultural dilution in their communities.

Balanced pragmatists with mixed views. They recognize both potential benefits (labor, economic contribution) and harms (competition, social strain) of immigration, seeing the issue as complex rather than clearly positive or negative.

Humanitarian-minded individuals open to diversity. Despite economic concerns, they view immigrants as people seeking better lives and believe immigration can bring cultural and economic benefits to the country.

Skeptical citizens disillusioned with national institutions. Given their deep distrust in government and pessimism about the country's decline, they doubt the government can manage immigration effectively or that immigrants would help a struggling nation.

Rural agricultural workers and informal sector laborers with minimal access to banking infrastructure. They conduct nearly all transactions in cash because digital payment systems are unavailable or unaffordable in their communities.

Small business owners and market vendors in urban and semi-urban areas who use cash for most transactions but occasionally accept digital payments from customers. They see digital payments as useful but not essential to their operations.

Salaried employees and professionals in formal employment who receive wages via bank transfer and use debit cards or digital wallets for regular purchases. They conduct roughly half their transactions digitally and half in cash depending on the merchant.

Young urban professionals and middle-class individuals with stable incomes who actively use credit cards, debit cards, and QR code payments for most purchases. They view digital payments as convenient and increasingly prefer them over cash.

Remittance recipients and families with relatives abroad who use digital transfer services and mobile money platforms for receiving funds, then convert to cash for daily expenses. They have moderate digital payment adoption driven by necessity rather than preference.
Traditional conservatives who are skeptical of immigration and believe immigrants pose social risks including higher crime rates. They prefer defending established traditions and habits.
Moderate traditionalists who have some concerns about immigration and crime but are not strongly convinced of a direct causal link. They lean toward tradition but acknowledge complexity.
Pragmatic centrists who are open to diversity and skeptical of sweeping generalizations about immigrants and crime. They see evidence as mixed and resist stereotyping.
Progressive liberals who strongly reject the claim that immigrants increase crime, viewing it as a harmful stereotype. They strongly prefer openness to diverse traditions and habits.

Disengaged citizens who feel uncertain about the relationship between immigration and crime due to limited political engagement and low confidence in public discourse. They may hold varied views without strong conviction.
Progressive egalitarians who strongly reject traditional gender roles. They believe women and men should have equal opportunities in all spheres of life, including work and home responsibilities.

Modern pragmatists who disagree with strict gender role separation but aren't strongly ideological about it. They see both men and women as capable of working and managing households based on individual choice and circumstances.

Moderate traditionalists who somewhat agree that traditional gender divisions have merit but acknowledge modern realities. They may prefer traditional arrangements but don't strongly oppose women working or men sharing domestic duties.

Conservative traditionalists who believe in clear gender role separation with men as primary breadwinners and women focused on home and family. They view this as a natural and beneficial social arrangement.
Ambivalent or indifferent respondents who haven't formed strong opinions on this issue. They may see merit in both traditional and modern approaches depending on individual circumstances.

Pragmatic Independents (35%): Self-employed professionals who view political parties as tools for business interests rather than ideological homes. They engage with politics transactionally and don't feel a strong personal connection to any party.

Disillusioned Skeptics (28%): Individuals deeply mistrustful of government and political institutions (reflecting the 70% with little/no trust in government). They deliberately avoid identifying with parties as an act of resistance against a system they see as corrupt.

Progressive Aligned (20%): Self-employed individuals with liberal values (evidenced by 67% disagreeing that women should stay home) who identify with left-leaning or center-left parties that align with their social views and economic interests.

Conservative Traditionalists (12%): Those holding traditional values (32% agree women should concentrate at home) who feel close to right-wing or conservative parties that represent their worldview on social and economic matters.

Apolitical Pragmatists (5%): Self-employed individuals focused entirely on business survival and personal satisfaction (73% quite satisfied with life) who simply don't engage with party politics as it seems irrelevant to their daily concerns.

Disillusioned urbanites with low institutional trust: These Lima residents are deeply pessimistic about their life satisfaction, having lost faith in political institutions and fearing consequences for speaking out. They see themselves as trapped in a system that doesn't serve them.

Pragmatic moderates managing expectations: These residents maintain modest life satisfaction by keeping expectations realistic and focusing on personal/family stability rather than systemic change. They accept things as they are without deep optimism or despair.

Socially progressive but economically anxious: These Lima dwellers lean toward openness on social issues like immigration and same-sex marriage, but their life satisfaction is tempered by economic concerns and skepticism about whether society is actually improving for people like them.

Tradition-oriented and cautiously content: These residents prefer defending established traditions and habits, and they tend toward slightly higher life satisfaction by finding meaning in cultural continuity and community values, though they remain wary of rapid change.

Rare optimists with institutional engagement: A small segment maintains genuine life satisfaction and some trust in institutions, possibly through political party affiliation or belief that gradual progress is occurring despite systemic challenges.
Progressive urban professionals who support LGBTQ+ rights and view same-sex marriage as a matter of equality and personal freedom. They strongly agree with marriage equality.
Moderate centrists who accept same-sex marriage as a legitimate choice, though they may not be strongly passionate about it. They agree with the statement.
Religious traditionalists influenced by Catholic values who believe marriage should be between a man and woman, viewing same-sex marriage as contrary to their faith. They disagree with the statement.

Conservative social traditionalists who oppose same-sex marriage based on traditional family values and social norms, though not necessarily from religious conviction. They strongly disagree with the statement.
Pragmatic fence-sitters who are uncertain or indifferent about same-sex marriage, neither strongly supporting nor opposing it based on live-and-let-live attitudes.

Pragmatic Believers: Catholics with moderate trust in institutions who accept traditional gender roles but support women's equality in employment. They tend toward cautious optimism about life despite concerns about national stagnation, finding satisfaction in family and faith.

Socially Progressive Skeptics: Younger, more educated Panamanians who reject traditional gender hierarchies and support LGBTQ+ equality, but feel pessimistic about the country's decline and their personal prospects, leading to lower life satisfaction despite progressive values.

Traditional Conservatives: Older, religiously devout Catholics with strong institutional trust who hold traditional views on gender roles and same-sex relationships. They maintain moderate life satisfaction grounded in religious faith and family, though concerned about national decline.

Disengaged Cynics: Politically disconnected Panamanians who see the country in decline and feel little trust in institutions or the Church. They struggle with life satisfaction due to economic concerns and lack of hope, regardless of their social views.

Satisfied Moderates: Middle-ground Panamanians who balance traditional Catholic values with moderate social views, maintain some institutional trust, and despite acknowledging national stagnation, report reasonable life satisfaction through personal resilience and community ties.

Progressive urbanites who embrace diversity and openness. They support same-sex marriage as part of accepting diverse traditions and lifestyles, viewing it as a matter of personal freedom and equality.

Moderate pragmatists with mixed views on tradition and modernity. They may accept same-sex marriage as a legal reality while having some personal reservations, or they see it as neither particularly good nor bad for society.

Traditional-minded citizens who prioritize conventional values and habits. They disagree with same-sex marriage based on religious or cultural beliefs about what marriage should be, though they may not feel strongly opposed.

Conservative believers with strong religious convictions. They strongly disagree with same-sex marriage, viewing it as contrary to their faith and traditional family values that they see as fundamental to society.

Disengaged citizens with low political interest and weak party affiliation. They have not formed strong opinions on same-sex marriage and may respond based on whatever cultural messaging they encounter most frequently.
Progressive urbanites who embrace diversity and openness. They see traditional values as potentially limiting and believe society benefits from cultural pluralism and new perspectives.
Moderate centrists who value both tradition and openness. They appreciate their cultural heritage but recognize the importance of adapting to a changing world and accepting diverse viewpoints.

Conservative traditionalists who prioritize preserving Uruguayan customs and established social norms. They worry that excessive openness to diversity threatens the cohesion and identity of their community.
Pragmatic pluralists who support diversity primarily for economic and practical reasons. They see openness to different traditions as beneficial for the country's development and competitiveness.
Ambivalent citizens who feel torn between respecting tradition and accepting change. They struggle to choose between these values and may shift their views depending on context.

Disillusioned pragmatists who have experienced economic hardship and insecurity firsthand. They see the country in decline due to deteriorating conditions, crime, and lack of opportunity, and this pessimism shapes their willingness to consider authoritarian alternatives.

Cautiously optimistic entrepreneurs and small business owners who believe the country is progressing despite challenges. They focus on personal economic gains and opportunities they've created for themselves through self-employment.

Socially conservative citizens concerned about moral decline and traditional values. They view the country as in decline due to what they perceive as erosion of family structures and religious influence, though they may see some economic progress.

Politically anxious individuals caught between hope and fear. They're uncertain whether the country is progressing or declining, worried about expressing their true views due to safety concerns, and conflicted about the direction of governance.

Idealistic progressives who believe the country could progress if institutions improved and society became more inclusive. They see current stagnation but maintain hope for positive change, though they remain a minority voice.
Disillusioned non-aligned citizens who have lost faith in political institutions and see no party representing their interests, reflecting the widespread distrust in leadership evident in the group.
Pragmatic party supporters who maintain some connection to a political party despite concerns about corruption and institutional weakness, seeking representation within the existing system.
Cautious civic participants who avoid strong political affiliations due to fear of negative consequences for speaking out, preferring to stay under the radar politically.
Progressive-minded citizens who feel close to parties aligned with openness to diversity and social inclusion, though they may share concerns about institutional effectiveness.
Traditional-oriented individuals who identify with conservative parties defending established values and habits, representing a smaller but distinct segment of the group.

Moderate progressives satisfied with democratic institutions. They tend to trust the president somewhat, viewing him as a legitimate representative of their center-left values and democratic processes.

Pragmatic centrists with conditional trust. They have some trust in the president but remain cautious, evaluating his performance on specific policies rather than offering blanket support or opposition.
Skeptical critics from across the political spectrum. They have little trust in the president, believing he has failed to deliver on promises or represents interests contrary to their own.
Disaffected citizens with deep institutional distrust. They have no trust in the president, viewing him as part of a broader political system that fails to represent ordinary people's interests.

Engaged progressives with strong institutional confidence. They have considerable trust in the president, aligning with his progressive agenda on social issues and believing he represents genuine democratic change.
Secular-minded progressives who view the Church with skepticism due to its traditional stances on gender roles and social issues; they tend to have little to no trust in religious institutions.

Moderate believers who maintain some cultural connection to Catholicism but are not particularly devout; they have some trust in the Church as a social institution despite disagreements on specific issues.
Practicing Catholics with strong faith who trust the Church's moral authority and role in society; they see it as an important spiritual and community institution.
Disillusioned former believers or those with negative personal experiences with the Church who have little trust; they may respect its historical role but question its current relevance and ethics.
Pragmatic middle-ground citizens who neither strongly trust nor distrust the Church, viewing it as one institution among many with both positive and negative aspects.
Devout traditionalists who view same-sex adoption as contrary to religious teachings and traditional family values. They strongly oppose this practice based on their faith convictions.
Religious moderates who hold traditional beliefs but recognize the complexity of the issue and believe same-sex couples could be adequate parents, though they may have some reservations.
Progressive believers who reconcile their faith with more inclusive views, believing that love and capability matter more than the gender composition of a couple seeking to adopt.
Pragmatists focused on child welfare who support same-sex adoption primarily because they believe children benefit from stable, loving homes regardless of parental gender.
Conflicted individuals who struggle between their religious upbringing and evolving social attitudes, uncertain about their position on this issue.

Progressive urbanites who value openness and diversity. They see traditional restrictions as limiting personal freedom and believe Peru benefits from embracing different cultural perspectives and lifestyles.

Moderate pragmatists who appreciate both tradition and change. They want to preserve important cultural values while remaining open to new ideas, seeing no inherent conflict between respecting heritage and accepting diversity.

Tradition-focused conservatives who prioritize maintaining Peru's established customs and social norms. They worry that excessive openness to diverse traditions threatens social cohesion and cultural identity.

Socially conservative but economically pragmatic young people from rural or religious backgrounds. They lean toward defending traditions but show some flexibility, recognizing that Peru is changing and younger generations have different values.

Disengaged or conflicted youth who feel uncertain about this question. Given the high distrust in institutions and concerns about speaking freely, some young Peruvians may avoid taking strong positions on cultural issues.
Progressive urban professionals in Bogotá who reject gender discrimination and believe women deserve equal job opportunities regardless of economic conditions.
Moderate centrists who disagree with the statement but without strong conviction, viewing gender equality as important though perhaps not their primary concern.
Traditional-minded residents who agree that men should have employment priority during economic hardship, reflecting conventional gender role beliefs.
Economically anxious individuals who strongly agree with male job priority, seeing this as practical protection for male breadwinners during scarce employment.
Ambivalent respondents with mixed views who neither strongly agree nor disagree, uncertain about balancing gender equality with economic pragmatism.

Progressive urbanites who embrace cultural diversity and see tradition as potentially limiting. They value openness to new ideas and ways of living, reflecting Uruguay's relatively liberal social attitudes on issues like same-sex marriage.

Moderate centrists who appreciate both tradition and openness, seeing them as complementary rather than opposed. They want to preserve what works from their cultural heritage while remaining pragmatically open to beneficial changes.

Tradition-conscious conservatives who prioritize maintaining established social structures and cultural continuity. They worry that excessive openness to diverse traditions could erode community cohesion and national identity.

Pragmatic middle-ground voters who don't strongly identify with either position and see merit in balancing tradition with selective openness. They tend toward cautious acceptance of diversity without ideological commitment.

Strong traditionalists who firmly believe society should defend established customs and habits against what they see as destabilizing cultural changes. They represent a small but vocal minority concerned about rapid social transformation.
Traditional conservatives who strongly oppose same-sex marriage on religious or cultural grounds, viewing it as contrary to family values
Moderate traditionalists who have reservations about same-sex marriage but aren't strongly opposed, preferring to maintain conventional definitions while respecting others
Pragmatic moderates who accept same-sex marriage as a matter of personal freedom and equal rights, though it may not align with their personal traditions
Progressive supporters who strongly believe in marriage equality as a fundamental right and actively support same-sex marriage
Indifferent or conflicted individuals who haven't formed strong opinions on the issue and may be influenced by social context or personal experiences
Conservative traditionalists who prioritize preserving Peruvian cultural values and social norms. They view rapid social change with concern and believe traditions provide important social stability.
Moderate conservatives who appreciate traditions but recognize some value in gradual openness to different perspectives. They seek a balance between cultural preservation and modest social evolution.

Progressive-leaning citizens who favor openness to diverse traditions and habits, seeing cultural pluralism as enriching society. They are more comfortable with social change and different ways of living.

Pragmatic centrists who don't strongly identify with either position, viewing both tradition and diversity as having merit depending on context. They tend toward moderate satisfaction with current arrangements.
Socially liberal advocates who strongly prefer diversity and openness, viewing traditional constraints as limiting individual freedom and social progress. They actively support cultural pluralism.
Traditional values prioritizers who believe men should have employment priority during scarcity, viewing this as natural gender roles aligned with family structures and Dominican cultural norms.
Moderate traditionalists who lean toward men having some preference in scarce job markets, though they acknowledge women's economic needs and don't feel strongly about it.
Egalitarian-minded women who strongly reject gender-based job discrimination, believing women deserve equal employment rights regardless of economic conditions.
Pragmatic moderates who see merit in both perspectives but ultimately believe job allocation should be based on qualifications rather than gender.
Progressive advocates who view male job preference as discriminatory and outdated, actively opposing any policy that would disadvantage women economically.
Devout traditionalists concerned about social order who believe immigrants strain public safety and resources, viewing crime as a legitimate concern tied to rapid demographic change.
Religious moderates who acknowledge immigration challenges but distinguish between correlation and causation, believing immigrants are not inherently more criminal than native Venezuelans.
Faith-driven humanitarians guided by Christian values of compassion who strongly reject the stereotype that immigrants increase crime, seeing it as unfair prejudice against vulnerable populations.
Pragmatic believers who recognize Venezuela's own severe crime problems and attribute them to systemic failure rather than immigration, skeptical that immigrants are the primary driver.
Conflicted devout citizens who feel torn between religious teachings on welcoming strangers and personal safety concerns in a country experiencing significant violence and instability.

Institutionalist centrists who value democratic structures and believe political parties are essential mechanisms for organizing representation and preventing authoritarianism, reflecting Argentina's historical experience with institutional collapse.

Disillusioned moderates skeptical of parties due to corruption and ineffectiveness, yet uncertain whether democracy can truly function without them, representing the ambivalence shown in the low party affiliation rates.

Anti-establishment reformers who believe democracy can work through direct participation and alternative mechanisms beyond traditional parties, appealing to those frustrated with Argentina's political stagnation.
Pragmatic centrists who acknowledge parties' flaws but see them as necessary evils for maintaining democratic order and preventing chaos, balancing idealism with realism.
Idealistic democrats who envision participatory democracy without intermediary party structures, though this view remains minority given Argentina's institutional context.

Progressive-leaning secular Venezuelans who support LGBTQ+ rights and believe sexual orientation has no bearing on parenting ability. They strongly agree that homosexual couples are equally good parents.

Moderate pragmatists who accept same-sex couples as parents based on individual capability rather than ideology, though they may have some reservations. They agree that homosexual couples are equally good parents.

Culturally conservative but not deeply religious Venezuelans who have doubts about same-sex parenting but aren't strongly opposed, reflecting ambivalence rather than conviction. They disagree with the statement.

Traditional-minded individuals who believe parenting is fundamentally tied to heterosexual family structures and strongly reject the idea that same-sex couples are equally capable parents. They strongly disagree.

Undecided or conflicted Venezuelans who haven't formed strong opinions on this issue, possibly due to limited exposure or competing values. They are scattered across disagree and strongly disagree categories.
Religious traditionalists with strong Catholic faith who view the Church as a moral authority and community pillar, especially important given Venezuela's spiritual needs during crisis.
Moderate believers who appreciate the Church's social work and humanitarian efforts but maintain some distance from institutional religion and its positions on social issues.
Secular-leaning progressives who respect the Church's charitable work but are skeptical of its influence on politics and social policy, particularly regarding LGBTQ+ rights and gender issues.
Disillusioned citizens who have lost faith in institutions generally, including the Church, due to Venezuela's political and economic crisis and perceived institutional failures.
Pragmatic believers who trust the Church primarily for its practical social services and community support during hardship, rather than for spiritual or moral guidance.

Pessimistic traditionalists who see the country in decline and distrust institutions. They worry about immigration and social changes, and have little to no trust in the president as a symbol of failed leadership.

Cautious moderates concerned about national direction but not entirely dismissive of leadership. They see mixed results from the government and have some trust in the president, though tempered by concerns about progress.

Pragmatic skeptics who believe the country is stagnating rather than declining. They hold moderate views on social issues and have little trust in the president, viewing him as ineffective rather than malicious.

Progressive optimists who believe the country is progressing despite challenges. They are more open to diversity and social change, and maintain some trust in the president as an agent of improvement.
Disengaged critics with no trust in the president whatsoever. They see the country in decline, hold traditional values, and view the political system as fundamentally broken regardless of who leads.

Cautiously optimistic progressives (21% of group): Moderate left-leaners who see some genuine improvements in Ecuador despite challenges, particularly in social services and institutional development, and believe the country is slowly moving forward.

Frustrated stagnation believers (28% of group): Centrists and moderate conservatives who feel Ecuador has been stuck in place for years with recurring political crises, corruption, and lack of meaningful reform, seeing neither clear progress nor dramatic decline.

Pessimistic decline observers (26% of group): Right-leaning citizens who view Ecuador as deteriorating due to gang violence, economic instability, institutional weakness, and loss of security, believing the country is moving backward despite occasional policy announcements.

Pragmatic mixed-view moderates (18% of group): Centrists who acknowledge progress in some areas (education, infrastructure) while recognizing serious decline in others (security, governance), seeing an uneven and contradictory national trajectory.

Disengaged or uncertain citizens (7% of group): Those with low life satisfaction or weak political engagement who struggle to assess the country's direction clearly and may not have formed strong opinions on national progress.

Progressive urbanites who view immigration through an economic and humanitarian lens, seeing immigrants as contributors to society and cultural diversity. They tend to be more educated and cosmopolitan in outlook.

Pragmatic moderates who acknowledge both benefits and challenges of immigration, seeing it as a complex issue without clear-cut answers. They recognize immigrants' contributions but also worry about job competition and social services.
Economic nationalists concerned primarily about job scarcity and wages, viewing immigrants as potential competitors for limited employment opportunities in a stagnant economy.

Conservative traditionalists who harbor skepticism toward immigration, associating it with social problems and cultural disruption, though their concerns are often expressed cautiously rather than aggressively.

Socially conscious youth who recognize Colombia's own emigration history and diaspora, feeling empathy for immigrants while remaining uncertain about domestic capacity to absorb them given the country's economic challenges.
Conservative traditionalists who oppose same-sex adoption based on traditional family values and religious beliefs, viewing it as harmful to children and society.
Moderate conservatives who have reservations about same-sex adoption but aren't strongly opposed, seeing it as acceptable in some circumstances but preferring traditional family structures.
Pragmatic moderates who believe same-sex couples can be good parents and adoption should be based on individual capability rather than sexual orientation.
Progressive supporters who strongly believe same-sex couples have equal rights to adopt and that denying them this right is discriminatory.
Socially anxious self-employed individuals who worry about expressing support for same-sex adoption due to potential negative professional or social consequences in their communities.

Pragmatic Acceptors (35%): People who have managed to secure stable employment and housing despite economic constraints; they feel their basic needs are met and express modest satisfaction with life, viewing their situation as acceptable given Peru's broader economic challenges.

Struggling but Hopeful (25%): Individuals living paycheck-to-paycheck who acknowledge financial stress but maintain some optimism about personal or family prospects; they are not very satisfied with current life circumstances but haven't given up on improvement.

Disillusioned and Weary (22%): People deeply frustrated by Peru's stagnation and political dysfunction who feel trapped in their economic situation; they express low life satisfaction, viewing their circumstances as unlikely to improve given the country's decline.

Resilient Optimists (12%): Individuals who, despite modest means, maintain positive outlooks through strong family or community ties and cultural values; they express reasonable satisfaction with life by focusing on non-material sources of wellbeing.

Anxious Precariat (6%): People in highly unstable economic situations who fear losing what little they have; they express very low life satisfaction and worry constantly about their ability to maintain their current minimal standard of living.
Progressive urbanites who view immigration positively and reject stereotypes about crime. They see immigrants as contributors to society and believe claims about increased crime are xenophobic myths.

Pragmatic moderates who acknowledge immigration's complexities and don't attribute crime increases primarily to immigrants. They recognize multiple factors affect crime rates and resist simplistic narratives.

Security-concerned citizens who believe immigrants do increase crime rates, reflecting their experience with Venezuela's deteriorating security situation. They worry about strain on already-fragile institutions.

Skeptical fence-sitters uncertain about the immigration-crime connection, given Venezuela's broader institutional collapse and crime problems. They're unsure whether to blame immigrants or systemic failures.
Strong anti-immigrant hardliners who firmly believe immigrants are responsible for rising crime and pose a direct threat to national security and stability.

Traditional conservatives who prioritize preserving Dominican cultural and religious values, viewing tradition as essential to social stability and identity. They prefer societies that maintain established customs and are skeptical of rapid cultural change.

Moderate traditionalists who appreciate Dominican heritage but recognize the need for some openness to new perspectives, seeking a balance between respecting traditions and allowing gradual social evolution.
Progressive urbanites in larger cities who actively embrace diversity and openness to different traditions, viewing cultural pluralism as enriching and necessary for modern society.
Pragmatic centrists who are neither strongly attached to tradition nor strongly committed to diversity, taking a flexible approach depending on specific circumstances and practical outcomes.
Young, socially liberal individuals who strongly prefer openness to diverse traditions and habits, viewing traditional constraints as limiting personal freedom and social progress.
Progressive urbanites who embrace diversity and openness. They see traditional values as potentially limiting and believe society benefits from exposure to different cultures and ways of living.
Moderate centrists who value both tradition and openness. They appreciate their cultural heritage but recognize the importance of adapting to a changing world and respecting different perspectives.
Tradition-conscious conservatives who prioritize preserving Uruguayan customs and established social structures. They worry that excessive openness to diversity could erode important cultural values.
Pragmatic fence-sitters who don't strongly identify with either position. They see merit in maintaining traditions while also acknowledging that some openness to change is necessary.
Strong traditionalists who firmly believe society should defend established habits and resist rapid cultural change. They view traditional values as essential to social stability.
Traditional gender role supporters who believe men should prioritize breadwinning and women should focus on home responsibilities, viewing male job priority as natural and necessary.
Moderate traditionalists who somewhat agree that men deserve job preference during scarcity, reflecting cultural norms while not holding the view strongly.
Pragmatic egalitarians who disagree with gender-based job discrimination, believing jobs should go to the most qualified regardless of gender.
Strong gender equality advocates who strongly disagree with any form of employment discrimination, viewing equal opportunity as a fundamental right.
Conflicted or uncertain individuals who hold mixed views on gender roles, sometimes agreeing with traditional norms in some contexts while supporting equality in others.
Traditional Catholics who prioritize Church teachings and cultural values. They strongly oppose same-sex adoption as incompatible with Dominican religious and family traditions.
Conservative pragmatists who respect traditions but acknowledge social reality. They disagree with same-sex adoption but are less emotionally invested than strong traditionalists.
Moderate progressives who value both tradition and openness to diversity. They are conflicted or slightly disagree with same-sex adoption, seeing merit in both perspectives.
Liberal urbanites who prioritize individual rights and equality over traditional norms. They agree or strongly agree that same-sex couples should have adoption rights.

Socially progressive but cautious individuals who support LGBTQ+ rights in principle but worry about social backlash in Dominican society. They agree with same-sex adoption but with some reservations.
Devout traditionalists who view the Church as a moral anchor and source of stability in uncertain times; they maintain strong faith despite economic hardships and see the Church as trustworthy.
Moderate believers who appreciate the Church's social role and community presence but have some reservations about its institutional practices; they express cautious, qualified trust.
Skeptical pragmatists struggling with economic hardship who feel the Church hasn't adequately addressed their material needs; they trust the Church somewhat but question its priorities.

Disillusioned critics who have lost faith in major institutions including the Church due to corruption, inequality, and unfulfilled promises; they express little to no trust in religious institutions.
Secular-minded individuals who respect the Church's cultural role in Dominican society but maintain emotional distance from it; they neither strongly trust nor distrust the institution.
Progressive urbanites who support LGBTQ+ rights and believe in legal recognition of gender identity as a matter of personal freedom and dignity.
Moderate pragmatists who accept gender identity recognition but have some reservations about implementation details or prefer a more cautious approach.
Traditional conservatives with religious or cultural values who oppose legal recognition of sex change on ID documents, viewing it as contrary to biological reality.
Socially conservative individuals who strongly reject gender identity recognition on documents, seeing it as a threat to traditional family and social structures.
Apolitical or disengaged individuals who haven't formed strong opinions on this issue and may respond based on immediate social context or limited information.

Progressive urbanites who value diversity and economic dynamism. They see immigrants as beneficial for filling labor gaps, bringing cultural richness, and contributing to economic growth, viewing this as consistent with Uruguay's tradition of openness.

Pragmatic moderates concerned with balance and integration. They acknowledge immigrants can be beneficial but worry about adequate social services, housing, and job competition, seeing the issue as neither purely positive nor negative depending on implementation.

Working-class Uruguayans feeling economic pressure and job insecurity. They view immigrant arrival as potentially harmful to their employment prospects and wages, particularly in lower-skilled sectors where they compete directly.

Conservative Catholics prioritizing social cohesion and traditional community structures. While their faith emphasizes charity toward migrants, they worry about rapid cultural change and strain on existing social bonds and institutions.

Pessimistic citizens reflecting the 59% who see the country at a standstill. They view immigrants as either a burden on stagnant resources or, conversely, as a necessary injection for a country going nowhere, but generally lean toward skepticism.
Traditional conservatives who prioritize established norms and religious values. They strongly oppose legal recognition of sex change, viewing it as contrary to natural order and religious teaching.

Moderate traditionalists who respect tradition but show some pragmatism. They disagree with sex change recognition on ID documents but aren't strongly opposed, seeing it as a personal matter that shouldn't be officially endorsed.
Pragmatic centrists with mixed views on social issues. They have reservations about sex change recognition but acknowledge individual rights, making them somewhat conflicted on this specific policy.
Progressive-leaning individuals who support individual freedoms and diversity. They agree that ID documents should recognize sex change as a matter of personal identity and dignity.
Strong progressives committed to LGBTQ+ rights and social inclusion. They strongly agree that legal recognition of sex change is essential for equality and human rights.
Traditional values conservatives who prioritize cultural and religious norms. They strongly oppose same-sex adoption as incompatible with their vision of family and Dominican traditions.
Moderate conservatives with some reservations about same-sex adoption. They disagree with the practice but are not strongly opposed, viewing it as outside traditional norms without being hostile.

Pragmatic moderates who accept same-sex couples but have concerns about adoption specifically. They agree somewhat that same-sex couples deserve recognition but worry about children's welfare or social integration.
Progressive supporters of LGBTQ+ rights who believe same-sex couples are equally capable parents. They strongly agree that adoption rights should be extended regardless of sexual orientation.

Socially liberal but cautious individuals who agree in principle with equality but remain uncertain about adoption. They support the idea but with reservations about implementation or social readiness.

Pragmatic moderates who view Venezuela with cautious concern but recognize complex geopolitical realities; they hold somewhat unfavorable views based on economic and humanitarian reports but avoid extreme positions.

Left-leaning sympathizers who maintain somewhat favorable views of Venezuela's anti-imperialist stance and social programs despite acknowledging governance challenges; they distrust Western media narratives.
Conservative critics who hold very unfavorable opinions of Venezuela's government due to concerns about authoritarianism, economic collapse, and socialist policies that conflict with their values.
Disengaged citizens with little strong opinion either way, viewing Venezuela as a distant issue with somewhat unfavorable leanings based on general awareness of the country's difficulties.
Regional solidarity advocates who maintain somewhat favorable views rooted in Latin American solidarity and anti-American sentiment, despite reservations about specific policies.

Conservative traditionalists who strongly oppose same-sex marriage based on religious and cultural values deeply rooted in Peruvian society. They view marriage as a traditional institution between man and woman.

Moderate traditionalists who have reservations about same-sex marriage but are not strongly opposed, preferring to maintain traditional definitions while showing some tolerance. They tend to disagree rather than strongly disagree.
Progressive urban professionals and younger people who support same-sex marriage as a matter of equality and individual rights, viewing it as compatible with modern values and human dignity.
Pragmatic moderates who are somewhat indifferent to the issue or see it as a personal matter that shouldn't be heavily regulated, neither strongly supporting nor opposing same-sex marriage.
Strong advocates for LGBTQ+ rights who strongly agree with same-sex marriage as a fundamental right and actively support legal recognition and equality.

Conservative traditionalists with deep institutional trust. They distrust democratic institutions and would support military intervention, view Venezuela negatively as a failed socialist state that threatens regional stability, and see it as a cautionary tale of leftist governance.

Pragmatic centrists concerned about governance and institutional performance. They have mixed views on Venezuela, recognizing both the humanitarian crisis and some past social programs, but ultimately view it unfavorably due to economic collapse and authoritarianism.

Democratic-minded progressives who value institutional pluralism and openness. They view Venezuela unfavorably but with some sympathy for its people and historical context, distinguishing between criticism of the government and the nation itself.

Disillusioned citizens with very low institutional trust across the board. They view Venezuela unfavorably primarily because they see it as emblematic of broader regional governance failures that mirror Honduras's own problems.

Left-leaning or sympathetic observers who maintain some favorable or neutral views of Venezuela despite its current difficulties. They may see it as a victim of external pressure or view it through an ideological lens that resists wholesale condemnation.
Tradition-focused pessimists who prioritize defending Honduras's established ways and believe immigrants strain resources and job opportunities, viewing their arrival as harmful to the country.
Pragmatic skeptics who are neither strongly pro- nor anti-immigration, seeing both potential benefits and drawbacks, and believe the impact is neither clearly beneficial nor harmful.
Open-minded progressives who value diversity and believe immigrants contribute economically and culturally to Honduras, viewing their arrival as beneficial despite current national challenges.
Disillusioned citizens experiencing economic hardship who blame immigrants for competing for scarce jobs and resources in a country they see as declining, viewing immigration as harmful.
Cautious moderates who recognize Honduras's economic struggles and worry about absorbing more people, leaning toward viewing immigration as harmful but without strong conviction.
Traditional gender role supporters who believe women's primary place is in the home while men should be breadwinners, reflecting conservative family values common in Guatemalan society.
Moderate traditionalists who somewhat agree with traditional gender divisions but acknowledge women can work, representing a compromise position between traditional and modern views.
Gender equality advocates who strongly reject the idea that women should concentrate at home, believing both men and women should have equal freedom to choose their roles.
Pragmatic moderates who disagree with the statement but not strongly, recognizing economic necessity often requires women to work despite traditional preferences.
Strongly progressive individuals who firmly oppose traditional gender role restrictions and view them as outdated constraints on human potential and freedom.

Institutional Trust Believers - These individuals maintain confidence in government institutions and believe the National Government deserves substantial trust. They tend to be more optimistic about governance and institutional effectiveness.

Cautious Moderates - These people have some trust in the National Government but remain skeptical, viewing it as partially functional but needing improvement. They represent a middle ground between optimism and cynicism.

Disappointed Skeptics - These individuals have little trust in the National Government, believing it has failed to deliver on key promises or represent their interests effectively. They are disillusioned but not entirely hopeless.

Institutional Rejectionists - These people have no trust in the National Government whatsoever, viewing it as corrupt, ineffective, or fundamentally broken. They represent deep alienation from state institutions.

Tradition-Oriented Institutional Supporters - These individuals combine their preference for traditional values and habits with relatively higher trust in established institutions like government. They see the National Government as a guardian of social order.

Pragmatic moderates concerned about economic stagnation. They see Guatemala as stuck in place, neither clearly progressing nor declining, but frustrated with slow institutional change and lack of opportunity.
Pessimistic traditionalists who believe the country is in decline due to moral decay, loss of values, and deteriorating security. They worry that social changes are making things worse.

Cautious optimists who see some progress in specific areas like education or infrastructure, but acknowledge significant challenges remain. They believe Guatemala is slowly moving forward despite obstacles.
Frustrated reformers who view the country as fundamentally stalled by corruption and institutional failure, believing real progress requires major systemic change or even authoritarian intervention.
Rural or marginalized citizens with limited engagement in national discourse, who see their immediate circumstances as difficult but lack clear perspective on national trajectory.
Progressive Catholics who embrace modern values and see diversity as enriching society. They value openness to different traditions and habits as essential to contemporary life.

Moderate traditionalists who appreciate their own cultural heritage but recognize the value of respecting other traditions. They seek a balance between preserving what matters and accepting social change.
Conservative Catholics for whom defending traditional Uruguayan and Catholic customs is paramount. They worry that excessive openness to diverse traditions threatens social cohesion and moral values.

Pragmatic citizens who care more about economic and political stability than cultural debates. They may lean either way depending on whether they see tradition or diversity as more practical for society.
Conflicted individuals who value both their traditions and respect for others, finding it difficult to choose between these two statements as they see merit in both positions.
Traditional cash-reliant workers in informal economy. Primarily use cash for daily transactions and are uncomfortable with or lack access to digital payment infrastructure.
Cautious digital adopters with mixed payment methods. Use digital payments for some regular expenses like utilities or groceries but still rely heavily on cash for most daily purchases.
Balanced digital users who split their transactions evenly. Comfortable with both digital and cash payments and use them interchangeably depending on convenience and merchant availability.
Regular digital payment users in formal employment. Primarily use cards and digital methods for most purchases but occasionally use cash for small transactions or informal vendors.
Fully digitalized urban professionals. Conduct nearly all financial transactions digitally through cards, apps, and QR codes with minimal cash usage.

Committed party loyalists with strong institutional trust. These individuals have deep connections to established political parties, often through family tradition or church networks, and feel a clear sense of political belonging.

Pragmatic party supporters motivated by specific policies or candidates. They feel close to a party because it addresses their concerns about jobs, security, or traditional values, but their loyalty is conditional on performance.

Disillusioned skeptics with low institutional trust. Given the 30% with no trust in government and widespread concerns about negative consequences for free speech, these people have withdrawn from party identification due to corruption or ineffectiveness.

Socially conservative evangelicals seeking moral alignment. They identify with parties that defend traditional values and religious interests, reflecting the 60% preference for tradition-defending societies.

Politically disengaged or undecided citizens. These individuals lack strong party affiliation because they feel disconnected from politics, uncertain about their views, or believe parties don't represent their interests.

Politically engaged progressives who feel connected to left-leaning parties aligned with recent social reforms and are actively involved in political discourse despite concerns about expressing themselves freely.
Moderate centrists who maintain some affinity with traditional or center parties but express cautious, conditional support rather than strong partisan loyalty.
Disillusioned youth skeptical of all political parties due to corruption, inequality, and unfulfilled promises, preferring to stay independent rather than commit to any political movement.
Conservative voters who identify with right-leaning or traditional parties but represent a smaller segment of this young demographic, often concerned about social stability.
Apolitical or disengaged individuals who lack interest in party politics altogether, viewing political affiliation as irrelevant to their daily lives.

Religious traditionalists with strong Church ties who view sex change recognition as contrary to religious and natural law principles, and believe traditional identity documents should reflect biological reality.

Social conservatives who are uncomfortable with sex change recognition but not primarily motivated by religious conviction; they see it as a modern trend that goes against established social norms and traditional family values.
Pragmatic moderates who acknowledge the reality of transgender individuals and see some merit in allowing ID recognition, but have reservations about implementation or broader social implications.
Progressive-minded individuals who support sex change recognition in ID documents as a matter of personal rights and dignity, viewing it as a humanitarian issue aligned with individual freedom.
Rights-focused advocates who strongly support ID recognition for sex change as a fundamental human right and necessary protection for vulnerable populations, seeing opposition as discriminatory.
Traditional-minded women who prioritize preserving Honduran cultural values and social stability, viewing openness to diverse traditions as a threat to family and community cohesion.
Pragmatic conservatives who respect traditions but recognize that some openness to different perspectives can coexist with maintaining core cultural values.
Progressive-leaning women who actively embrace diversity and see openness to different traditions as essential for social progress and reducing discrimination.
Ambivalent moderates who see merit in both preserving traditions and accepting diversity, struggling to choose between the two competing values.
Cosmopolitan women with exposure to international perspectives who strongly prefer a society open to diverse traditions and view traditional-only approaches as limiting.

Disillusioned emigrants and their families who have experienced Venezuela's economic and political crisis firsthand, viewing the country with deep pessimism and harboring very unfavorable opinions due to personal hardship and loss.

Pragmatic middle-ground citizens who acknowledge Venezuela's serious problems but retain some hope for institutional recovery or gradual improvement, holding somewhat unfavorable views while not completely losing faith.
Government supporters and Chavista loyalists who maintain favorable views of Venezuela despite economic difficulties, seeing the country's direction as fundamentally sound and worthy of support.
Cautiously optimistic citizens who believe in Venezuela's potential and resources, viewing the country somewhat favorably while acknowledging current challenges as temporary or solvable.

Deeply committed nationalists with strong emotional attachment to Venezuela who maintain very favorable views rooted in cultural pride, historical significance, and belief in the nation's inherent greatness regardless of current circumstances.
Conservative traditionalists who strongly oppose same-sex adoption based on traditional family values and religious beliefs, viewing it as harmful to children.
Moderate conservatives who disagree with same-sex adoption but are not strongly opposed, seeing it as against traditional norms without being absolutist.
Pragmatic centrists who are neutral or see both merits and concerns in same-sex adoption, believing it's neither clearly beneficial nor harmful.
Progressive supporters who agree that same-sex couples can be good parents and should have adoption rights, viewing this as a matter of equality.
Strong advocates who strongly agree with same-sex adoption rights, seeing it as essential to LGBTQ+ equality and children's welfare.
Conservative traditionalists with strong religious faith who view immigration skeptically and believe immigrants pose security and social risks to their communities.
Moderately concerned citizens who acknowledge some connection between immigration and crime but recognize it's a complex issue with multiple factors involved.
Pragmatic working-class Guatemalans who have direct experience with migration (either as migrants themselves or with family abroad) and understand the nuances of immigrant experiences.
Socially progressive individuals, often younger and more educated, who reject stereotypes about immigrants and crime, viewing such claims as discriminatory generalizations.
Religiously devout individuals focused on Christian values of compassion and hospitality who believe in treating immigrants with dignity regardless of crime statistics.
Disillusioned working poor who see economic hardship and lack of opportunity in their daily lives, viewing the country as clearly in decline despite any official narratives.
Cautiously optimistic lower-middle class who have experienced some improvements in their circumstances and believe the country is slowly progressing, though progress feels fragile.
Politically engaged citizens who are deeply skeptical of institutions and see the country as stalled by corruption and political dysfunction, unable to move forward meaningfully.
Church-connected individuals with strong faith who maintain hope that the country can progress through moral and spiritual renewal, despite current challenges.
Young people with digital access who see mixed signals—some progress in technology and connectivity but decline in security and economic prospects for their generation.
Traditional conservatives who believe in conventional family structures and are uncomfortable with same-sex parenting, viewing it as fundamentally different from heterosexual parenting.
Moderate skeptics who have some reservations about same-sex parenting but aren't strongly opposed, reflecting uncertainty rather than firm conviction.
Pragmatic acceptors who believe that parenting ability depends on individual qualities like love and stability rather than parental gender or sexual orientation.
Strong progressives who actively support LGBTQ+ equality and firmly believe same-sex couples are equally capable parents as any other couples.
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who haven't formed strong opinions on this issue and may answer based on immediate social cues rather than deep conviction.

Progressive urbanites who embrace diversity and modern values. They strongly support same-sex marriage as a matter of equality and personal freedom, consistent with their openness to diverse traditions.

Moderate pragmatists who accept same-sex marriage as a legal reality and don't see it as threatening, though they may not be passionate advocates. They lean toward agreement but without strong conviction.

Traditional conservatives who hold reservations about same-sex marriage based on conventional family values, though they're not uniformly hostile. They tend toward disagreement but represent a minority position in this relatively progressive group.

Conflicted middle-grounders who are uncertain about same-sex marriage, torn between traditional upbringing and exposure to more liberal social attitudes. They may lean slightly toward disagreement or remain neutral.
Strong traditionalists who firmly oppose same-sex marriage on religious or cultural grounds and view it as contrary to established norms. They strongly disagree with this practice.

Pragmatic but weary workers: People with steady employment or family responsibilities who manage day-to-day life adequately but feel worn down by economic stagnation and lack of progress in the country. They are quite satisfied with their personal lives and relationships but not optimistic about broader circumstances.

Struggling and dissatisfied: People facing economic hardship, unemployment, or precarious work situations who feel the weight of the country's decline and their own limited opportunities. They are not very or not at all satisfied with their lives overall.

Content with modest circumstances: People who have accepted their station in life, maintain strong family and community ties, and find satisfaction in what they have rather than focusing on what they lack. They tend toward quite satisfied despite broader national concerns.

Optimistic and forward-looking: People who see possibilities for improvement, whether through personal effort or social change, and maintain a generally positive outlook on their lives. They are quite or very satisfied and believe progress is still possible.

Deeply dissatisfied and alienated: People who feel disconnected from society, pessimistic about both personal prospects and the country's future, and express low satisfaction across the board. They see decline everywhere and feel powerless to change it.

Economically struggling workers who view immigrants as competitors for scarce jobs and resources in an already difficult labor market, blaming immigration for worsening their family's financial situation.
Religious traditionalists with strong Church ties who see immigration through a humanitarian lens rooted in Christian values, viewing immigrants as people in need deserving of compassion and support.
Pragmatists who recognize both challenges and benefits of immigration, acknowledging that while immigrants may compete for jobs, they also contribute to society and fill labor gaps.
Politically cautious individuals who fear expressing strong opinions on immigration due to concerns about government repercussions, leading them to adopt neutral or ambivalent positions.
Socially progressive minorities who support immigration based on principles of human rights and solidarity, viewing immigrants as fellow people deserving dignity regardless of economic impacts.
Progressive urbanites with secular values who support LGBTQ+ rights and see same-sex marriage as a matter of personal freedom and equality, regardless of religious tradition.
Moderate pragmatists who accept same-sex marriage as a civil right even if they have personal reservations, viewing it as inevitable social progress that deserves legal recognition.

Traditional conservatives who disagree with same-sex marriage based on cultural and religious grounds, believing marriage should remain between a man and a woman, though they may tolerate LGBTQ+ people.
Strong religious traditionalists who strongly oppose same-sex marriage as contrary to their faith and values, viewing it as a fundamental threat to family structure.

Apathetic or disengaged citizens who have not formed strong opinions on same-sex marriage and may answer based on whatever seems socially acceptable or default to traditional views without deep conviction.
Progressive urbanites who strongly reject traditional gender roles and believe women should have equal opportunities in all spheres of life, including work and career advancement.
Moderate egalitarians who disagree with strict gender role separation but may acknowledge some traditional perspectives exist, viewing gender equality as important but not necessarily extreme.
Pragmatic traditionalists who hold some traditional views about gender roles but are not strongly ideological about it, seeing both work and home as valid domains for men and women.
Conservative believers in traditional family structures who agree that women's primary role should be domestic while men focus on work, viewing this as natural and beneficial for families.
Disengaged or ambivalent respondents who have not formed strong opinions on gender role questions and may answer based on immediate circumstances rather than consistent ideology.

Traditional values conservatives who prioritize defending established customs and habits; they strongly disagree with same-sex marriage as it conflicts with their view of traditional family structures.
Moderate traditionalists who lean toward preserving traditions but are somewhat open to diversity; they disagree with same-sex marriage but without strong conviction.
Pragmatic moderates focused on practical concerns rather than ideological positions; they are neutral or slightly disagreeing on same-sex marriage, viewing it as a non-priority issue.
Progressive-leaning individuals who value openness to diverse traditions and habits; they agree with same-sex marriage as part of accepting social diversity.
Strong progressives who actively support LGBTQ+ rights and strongly agree that same-sex marriage should be accepted in society.

Authoritarian-leaning pragmatists who have shown openness to military government and see political parties as unnecessary obstacles to effective governance. They believe democracy can function without parties if a strong leader can deliver results.

Disengaged citizens with low political party affiliation who are skeptical of traditional democratic institutions. They see parties as corrupt or ineffective and believe alternative forms of governance could work without them.

Traditional conservatives who support conventional democratic structures including political parties, viewing them as essential safeguards against authoritarianism. They reject military alternatives and believe parties are necessary for democracy.

Socially progressive but politically detached individuals who support democratic values and gender equality but feel alienated from existing political parties. They are uncertain whether parties are truly necessary for democracy to function.

Institutional democrats who strongly believe in the necessity of political parties as fundamental to democratic representation and accountability. They view parties as essential checks on power regardless of other political views.
Pessimistic traditionalists who feel the country is declining due to economic hardship, crime, and loss of values; they may support authoritarian solutions and distrust institutions.
Cautiously hopeful pragmatists who see some progress in certain areas but acknowledge significant stagnation in addressing core problems like employment and security.
Frustrated stagnation believers who feel the country is stuck in place, neither improving nor worsening dramatically, with persistent unresolved issues.
Optimistic progressives who believe the country is moving forward despite challenges, maintaining faith in democratic institutions and gradual improvement.
Disengaged skeptics who are uncertain about the country's direction, focused primarily on personal life satisfaction rather than national trajectory.
